       \le\frac12\frac{\mu[f^2X^{\mathsf T}B_{p_1}X]}N,
 \qquad
 \log\frac{\,\mathrm d(Q_\mu|_{p_1})}{\,\mathrm dQ_0}(h)
       \ge-\frac12\mu[X^{\mathsf T}B_{p_1}X].$$ These formulas are on the range of $B_{p_1}$, so zero precision directions cause no difficulty. Subtraction bounds $D(Q_{\rm spin}|_{p_1}\Vert Q_\mu|_{p_1})$ by half the sum of the two quadratic moments. The spectral bound $d_1\ge-\epsilon_{\rm sp}p_1^2$ gives $B_{p_1}\preceq(1+\epsilon_{\rm sp})p_1^2P_{p_1}
\preceq2p_1^2P_{p_1}$. The projection tail in Proposition <a href="#prop:edge-estimates" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:edge-estimates">3</a>, integrated against a density at most $e^L$, gives $$\frac{\mu[f^2\|P_{p_1}X\|^2]}{NM_{p_1}^2}
       +\frac{\mu[\|P_{p_1}X\|^2]}{M_{p_1}^2}
 \le C\left(1+(L/k_{p_1})^{1/3}\right).$$ For example, integrate $\min\{1,e^LCe^{-c k_{p_1}v^6}\}$ in the variable $v^2$. The information is therefore at most $$Ck_{p_1}\left(1+(L/k_{p_1})^{1/3}\right)
   \le C(c_0+c_0^{2/3})L .$$ This is the proportional-cap argument in (OpenAI 2026b, Equation (19.12)) <a id="pm-cite-55"></a>[[CM](#ref-CM)]. Choose $c_0$ so that this last bound is less than $L/8$. The full spin-tilt entropy is at least $L/2$. The two continuity comparisons in <a href="#warm:entropy-continuity" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="warm:entropy-continuity">[warm:entropy-continuity]</a>, combined into one uniform $o(L)$, therefore give <a id="warm:residual-lower"></a>$$\label{warm:residual-lower}
 \begin{split}
 H(p_1)&\ge D(Q_{\rm spin}\Vert Q_\mu)
       -D(Q_{\rm spin}|_{p_1}\Vert Q_\mu|_{p_1})-o(L)\\
       &\ge L/2-L/8-o(L)\ge cL.
 \end{split}$$

<a id="warm:residual-transition-entropy"></a>
We follow that remaining entropy up to a fixed fraction of $R$. For $p<R$, let $\mathsf T_{p,R}^h$ be the ordinary conditional law of $h_R$ given $h_p=h$. It has density proportional to $$e^{\phi_R(y)}\,\mathcal N(h,B_R-B_p)(\,\mathrm dy),$$ where the Gaussian is restricted to the range of its covariance. Let $\widetilde{\mathsf T}_{p,R}^h$ be its tilt by $F_R(y)^2$, and put $$A_p(h)=\mathsf T_{p,R}^h[F_R^2],\qquad
 l_p(h)=D(\widetilde{\mathsf T}_{p,R}^h\Vert\mathsf T_{p,R}^h).$$ Observation sufficiency gives the prefix density $\,\mathrm d(Q_{\rm obs}|_p)/\,\mathrm d(Q_\mu|_p)=A_p(h_p)/A$. The conditional chain rule in <a href="#warm:residual-observation-entropy" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="warm:residual-observation-entropy">[warm:residual-observation-entropy]</a> now reads $$\label{warm:residual-transition-entropy}
 H(p)=\frac1A Q_\mu\!\left[
       \mathop{\mathrm{Ent}}_{\mathsf T_{p,R}^{h_p}}(F_R^2)\right]
       =Q_{\rm obs}[l_p(h_p)].$$

<a id="warm:bridge-loss"></a>
Write $\Delta=B_R-B_p$. On the currently active subspace $\mathcal H_p$, $\Delta=(R^2-p^2)I$. Differentiating its Gaussian convolution therefore gives $$\nabla_{\mathcal H_p}\log A_p(h)=\delta m_h,\qquad
 \delta m_h=\widetilde{\mathsf T}_{p,R}^h[S]
                    -\mathsf T_{p,R}^h[S],\qquad
 S=\frac{P_p(h_R-h)}{R^2-p^2}.$$ In the parameter $p^2$, the likelihood martingale $A_p(h_p)/A$ has innovation coefficient $(A_p/A)\delta m_h$. The Gaussian likelihood formula for its relative entropy and the chain rule yield $$-\frac{\,\mathrm dH}{\,\mathrm d\log p}
      =p^2Q_{\rm obs}[|\delta m_h|^2] .                   \label{warm:bridge-loss}$$ This identity holds almost everywhere and in integrated form across activation points. One direct justification applies Itô’s formula to $(u+\epsilon)\log(u+\epsilon)$ of the bounded likelihood, then lets $\epsilon\downarrow0$; zero-rate directions are omitted. This is the observation entropy identity (OpenAI 2026b, Lemma 19.2, Equation (19.6)) <a id="pm-cite-56"></a>[[CM](#ref-CM)], applied here to a terminal observation tilt instead of a spin tilt.

<a id="warm:bridge-mean"></a>
The ordinary log moment generating function of $S$, for $v\in\mathcal H_p$, is exactly $$\log\mathsf T_{p,R}^h[e^{\langle v,S\rangle}]
   =\phi_p(h+v)-\phi_p(h)+\frac{|v|^2}{2(R^2-p^2)} .$$ Suppose that the Hessian of $\phi_p$ in this subspace is at most $C_{\rm curv}p^{-2}I$ on all shifts of length at most $p\sqrt{2l_p(h)/C_{\rm curv}}$ from $h$. The entropy variational inequality, tested against $\langle v,S\rangle$, then gives $$p^2|\delta m_h|^2
 \le2\left(C_{\rm curv}+\frac{p^2}{R^2-p^2}\right)l_p(h).
                                                               \label{warm:bridge-mean}$$ To check the finite shift radius, the centered log moment generating function is at most $\frac12(C_{\rm curv}p^{-2}+(R^2-p^2)^{-1})|v|^2$. Testing at length $\sqrt{2l_p/(C_{\rm curv}p^{-2}+(R^2-p^2)^{-1})}$ in the mean-shift direction proves the inequality by contradiction; this length is no larger than the assumed radius.

<a id="warm:bridge-entropy-tail"></a>
<a id="warm:bridge-input-tails"></a>
<a id="warm:discarded-bridge"></a>
We next account for observations where that curvature bound is not available. The entropy bound $l_p\le-\log A_p$, together with $A\ge e^{-L}/2$, implies $$Q_{\rm obs}(l_p>L+\log2+z)\le e^{-z},\qquad z\ge0.
                                                               \label{warm:bridge-entropy-tail}$$ Under the ordinary joint law, $$S=P_pX+(R^2-p^2)^{-1/2}G_p,$$ with an independent standard Gaussian $G_p$ on $\mathcal H_p$. For $p\le\gamma R$, the projection tails of Proposition <a href="#prop:edge-estimates" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:edge-estimates">3</a> and Gaussian concentration give, for each prescribed $a_0>0$, a fixed $V$ such that $$\label{warm:bridge-input-tails}
 \begin{split}
 Q_\mu\!\left[\frac{|S|^2}{M_p^2}
       \mathbf 1_{\{|S|>VM_p\}}\right]&\le Ce^{-a_0k_p},\\
 Q_\mu\{\|h_p\|>Vp^2M_p\}&\le Ce^{-a_0k_p}.
 \end{split}$$ To see the common scale, write the observation noise using a standard Gaussian $G'_p$ on $\mathcal H_p$. Since $B_p\preceq2p^2P_p$, $$\frac{\|h_p\|}{p^2M_p}
 \le2\frac{\|P_pX\|}{M_p}+\sqrt2\frac{\|G'_p\|}{\sqrt{k_p}},
 \qquad
 \frac{|S|}{M_p}
 \le\frac{\|P_pX\|}{M_p}
       +\frac p{\sqrt{R^2-p^2}}\frac{\|G_p\|}{\sqrt{k_p}}.$$ The last coefficient is bounded on this range and $\dim\mathcal H_p\le Ck_p$. Integration of the same tails allows any fixed polynomial moment as well. For a prefix event $E$, conditional Jensen and the full and prefix likelihood bounds at most $2e^L$ give $$\begin{split}
 p^2Q_{\rm obs}[|\delta m_h|^2\mathbf 1_E]
 \le Ck_p\bigg(
 V^2Q_{\rm obs}(E)
 +e^L Q_\mu\!\left[
       \frac{|S|^2}{M_p^2}\mathbf 1_{\{|S|>VM_p\}}\right]\bigg).
\end{split}                                                     \label{warm:discarded-bridge}$$ Indeed Jensen bounds $|\delta m_h|^2$ by twice the sum of the second moments under the two conditional laws. For their parts $|S|\le VM_p$ use the prefix probability of $E$; for the remaining parts use respectively the full likelihood $F_R^2/A$ and the prefix likelihood $A_p/A$. Finally $p^2M_p^2=k_p$.

Choose $p_2$ by $k_{p_2}=C_2k_{p_1}$, where $C_2$ will be fixed below. Once it is fixed, $p_2<\gamma R$ for $K_0$ sufficiently large. Fix $A_0>0$, choose a tail rate $a_0>c_0^{-1}$ with a fixed margin, and then choose $V$ in <a href="#warm:bridge-input-tails" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="warm:bridge-input-tails">[warm:bridge-input-tails]</a>. On $[p_1,p_2]$ retain $\|h_p\|\le Vp^2M_p$ and $l_p\le L+\log2+A_0k_p$. The trial shifts in <a href="#warm:bridge-mean" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="warm:bridge-mean">[warm:bridge-mean]</a>, in units $p^2M_p$, then have length at most $\sqrt{2(c_0^{-1}+A_0+1)}$, after enlarging the ball-curvature constant to be at least one. Choose a fixed ball containing the retained fields and these shifts before requesting its curvature constant from Proposition <a href="#prop:edge-estimates" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:edge-estimates">3</a>. Equations <a href="#warm:bridge-entropy-tail" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="warm:bridge-entropy-tail">[warm:bridge-entropy-tail]</a>–<a href="#warm:discarded-bridge" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="warm:discarded-bridge">[warm:discarded-bridge]</a> show that discarded observations contribute at most $Ck_pe^{-c k_p}$. Thus <a href="#warm:bridge-loss" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="warm:bridge-loss">[warm:bridge-loss]</a>–<a href="#warm:bridge-mean" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="warm:bridge-mean">[warm:bridge-mean]</a> imply $$\frac{\,\mathrm dH}{\,\mathrm d\log p}\ge-C_1H-Ck_pe^{-c k_p}
       \qquad(p_1\le p\le p_2).$$ The logarithmic length of this interval is fixed.

For $[p_2,\gamma R]$, make a fresh auxiliary cap and extension request with the same $\gamma$. Choose $\eta\ll\gamma^2$, then $\epsilon_{\rm aux}\le\epsilon$ sufficiently small compared with $\eta$. Reapply the construction of Lemma <a href="#edge:annular-extension" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="edge:annular-extension">13</a> with these choices, and write $s_0$ for its auxiliary width. Let $\mathcal G_{\rm ext}=\mathcal G_n^{\rm aux,ext}
\cap\mathcal G_n^{\rm FUA}$ be the resulting event for the required static tolerances, radii, threshold, and scale buffers. Lemma <a href="#edge:cube-caps" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="edge:cube-caps">10</a> gives $\mathcal G_n^{\rm aux,ext}$ with arbitrarily high limiting ordinary probability, and $\mathcal G_n^{\rm FUA}$ costs $o(1)$. Assign a further fraction of the failure probability and intersect with the retained variance event; its exponent $a$ and constants are unchanged.

<a id="warm:retained-small"></a>
On the full annulus $|\alpha_p(h)|\le s_0p^2$, this request gives $K_p(h)\preceq(1+\epsilon_{\rm aux})p^{-2}I
\preceq(1+\epsilon)p^{-2}I$. The same annulus specifies admissible child fields for the extension. Choose $0<\zeta<s_0$ and a fixed $b_{\rm rad}>0$ so that shifts of length at most $b_{\rm rad}p^2M_p$ from $|\alpha_p(h)|\le\zeta p^2$ stay in the full annulus. After $\zeta$ is fixed, impose its ordinary annulus estimate from Lemma <a href="#edge:path-annuli" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="edge:path-annuli">11</a> as one further fixed request and intersection. Thus the ordinary failure probability is $Ce^{-a_\zeta k_p}$, with a fixed $a_\zeta>0$; only this probability bound is used from the further request. The trial shifts fit whenever $l_p\le b k_p$, where $b=(1+\epsilon)b_{\rm rad}^2/2$. Choose $C_2$ so large that $$\frac{L}{k_p}\le\frac1{C_2c_0}
       <\frac14\min\{b,a_\zeta\}\qquad(p\ge p_2).$$ The likelihood bound and <a href="#warm:bridge-entropy-tail" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="warm:bridge-entropy-tail">[warm:bridge-entropy-tail]</a> give exponentially small tilted probabilities for both discarded events. Using <a href="#warm:discarded-bridge" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="warm:discarded-bridge">[warm:discarded-bridge]</a> with a further fixed $S$-tail threshold proves $$\frac{\,\mathrm dH}{\,\mathrm d\log p}
 \ge-\left(2(1+\epsilon)+\frac{2p^2}{R^2-p^2}\right)H
        -Ck_pe^{-c k_p}.$$ The extra coefficient has bounded integral, $$\int_{p_2}^{\gamma R}\frac{2p^2}{R^2-p^2}\,\,\mathrm d\log p
       \le-\log(1-\gamma^2).$$ In both intervals the integrating factor charges a fixed power of $p/p_1$, whereas $k_p=np^3$ grows as its cube. Consequently the weighted errors are bounded by a polynomial in $k_{p_1}$ times $(e^{-c k_{p_1}}+e^{-c k_{p_2}})$. They are $o(L)$ after increasing $K_0$. The first interval costs a fixed multiplicative factor. We obtain $$H(\gamma R)\ge cL(p_1/R)^{2+2\epsilon}.                  \label{warm:retained-small}$$

It remains to bound this entropy by the energy of $f$. For a child field satisfying $|\alpha_{\gamma R}(h)|\le s_0(\gamma R)^2$, the fresh request to Lemma <a href="#edge:annular-extension" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="edge:annular-extension">13</a> supplies an extension of the parent potential with upper Hessian $(1+\eta)R^{-2}I$. Put $$\mathcal A_R=\{|\alpha_R|\le s_0R^2/2\},\qquad
 \mathcal A_R^+=\{|\alpha_R|<3s_0R^2/4\}.$$ The extension agrees with the true potential on $\mathcal A_R^+$. The distance from $\mathcal A_R$ to $(\mathcal A_R^+)^c$ is at least $c_{\rm buf}R^2M_R$. Both transition laws assign $\mathcal A_R^c$ probability $Ce^{-c k_R}$, also with fixed polynomial moments of $\|h_R\|/(R^2M_R)$. The precision increment satisfies $\Delta\preceq(1-\gamma^2)R^2I$. On its range the extended transition, denoted by $\overline{\mathsf T}$, has negative log-density Hessian at least $$\Delta^{-1}-(1+\eta)R^{-2}I\succeq c_\gamma R^{-2}I .$$ The Bakry–Émery logarithmic Sobolev criterion (Bakry, Gentil, and Ledoux 2014, Corollary 5.7.2) <a id="pm-cite-57"></a>[[BakryGentilLedoux2014](#ref-BakryGentilLedoux2014)] gives $$\mathop{\mathrm{Ent}}_{\overline{\mathsf T}}(g^2)
\le C_\gamma R^2\overline{\mathsf T}[|\nabla g|^2].$$ It applies to the semiconcave extension by mollification.

<a id="warm:transition-lsi"></a>
Choose a smooth cutoff $\chi$ equal to one on $\mathcal A_R$ and supported in $\mathcal A_R^+$. The fixed buffer and the radial saddle derivative in Proposition <a href="#prop:edge-estimates" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:edge-estimates">3</a> give $|\nabla\chi|\le C/(R^2M_R)$. Apply the preceding inequality to $\chi F_R$. Its cutoff-gradient term is at most $Ce^{-c k_R}$, because $R^2|\nabla\chi|^2\le C/k_R$ and the transition tail has that exponential rate. On agreement the ratio of the two transition densities is constant; their normalization and their exponentially small tails make that constant $1+O(e^{-c k_R})$. To compare the entropies, use $\mathop{\mathrm{Ent}}_{\mathsf T}(g)=\mathsf T[g\log g]-\mathsf T[g]\log\mathsf T[g]$: $x\log x$ is bounded and Hölder continuous on $[0,1]$, and $0\le F_R,\chi\le1$. The comparison, with a possibly smaller positive exponent, proves $$\mathop{\mathrm{Ent}}_{\mathsf T_{\,\gamma R,R}^{h}}(F_R^2)
 \le C_\gamma R^2\mathsf T_{\,\gamma R,R}^{h}
                   [|\nabla_{\mathcal H_R}F_R|^2]+Ce^{-c k_R}.
                                                               \label{warm:transition-lsi}$$ Failure of the child condition is contained in the ordinary $\zeta$-annulus failure, since $\zeta<s_0$. Its probability is $Ce^{-c k_R}$ after changing $c$, since $k_{\gamma R}=\gamma^3k_R$. On it the conditional entropy of $F_R^2\le1$ is at most $1/e$. Average <a href="#warm:transition-lsi" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="warm:transition-lsi">[warm:transition-lsi]</a> under the ordinary child law and use <a href="#warm:residual-transition-entropy" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="warm:residual-transition-entropy">[warm:residual-transition-entropy]</a>. The tower property, $A\ge N/2$, and the two inequalities of <a href="#edge:variance-estimates" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="edge:variance-estimates">[edge:variance-estimates]</a> at $R$ give <a id="warm:small-upper"></a>$$\begin{split}
 H(\gamma R)
 &\le\frac{C_\gamma R^2}{A}
       Q_\mu\!\left[\|\nabla_{\mathcal H_R}F_R(h_R)\|^2\right]
       +\frac{Ce^{-c k_R}}A\\
 &\le C\frac{V_R}{N}+C\exp\{L-c k_R^a\}\\
 &\le C R^{-2}\frac{\mathcal E(f)}N+C\exp\{L-c k_R^a\}.
 \end{split}                                                \label{warm:small-upper}$$ Here $0<a\le1$ allows the transition error to be included in the displayed remainder, and $k_R=L^M$ makes it $C e^{L-cL^{Ma}}$. The error is negligible compared with <a href="#warm:retained-small" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="warm:retained-small">[warm:retained-small]</a>, even if the latter is a negative power of $L$. Comparing the two bounds and using $T_np_1^2=(c_0L)^{2/3}$ gives $$T_n\,\frac{\mathcal E(f)}N
 \ge c\,T_nR^2L(p_1/R)^{2+2\epsilon}
 =c' L^{5/3-2(M-1)\epsilon/3}.$$ The choice $2(M-1)\epsilon/3<\kappa$ contradicts the assumed upper bound for $K_0$ large. All ball radii, tail rates, annulus tolerances and factor buffers have been fixed before this last increase of $K_0$ and before $n$ tends to infinity. ◻

</details>

<a id="warm:large-section"></a>
#### The product endpoint and larger entropy levels

<a id="warm:spin-loss"></a>
<a id="warm:conditioned-energy"></a>
We record first two entropy bounds at a product posterior. Let $\nu=f^2\mu/N$. For each path used below, let $Q_\mu,Q_\nu$ denote the corresponding joint laws of the initial spin and its observations, started from these two spin laws. Expectations of observation-only functions use their observation marginals, and $Q|_u$ again denotes the observation prefix, excluding the spin. At observation time $u$, write $\mu_u,\nu_u$ for their spin posteriors and $N_u=\mu_u[f^2]$. Use the posterior heat-bath form and the weighted Euclidean norm $$\mathcal E_{\mu_u}(f)=\sum_i\mu_u[\mathop{\mathrm{Var}}_{\mu_u}(f\mid X_{-i})],
 \qquad \|v\|_A^2=v^{\mathsf T}Av.$$ Bayes’ formula and the observation identities of (OpenAI 2026b, Lemma 19.2, Equations (19.6)–(19.8)) <a id="pm-cite-58"></a>[[CM](#ref-CM)] are <a id="warm:posterior-likelihood"></a>$$\begin{aligned}
 \frac{\,\mathrm d(Q_\nu|_u)}{\,\mathrm d(Q_\mu|_u)}
       &=\frac{N_u}{N},\qquad \nu_u=\frac{f^2\mu_u}{N_u},
                                                               \label{warm:posterior-likelihood}\\
 -\dot H(u)
       &=\frac12 Q_\nu\!\left[
             \|\nu_u[X]-\mu_u[X]\|_{\dot B_u}^{\,2}\right],
 \qquad H(u)=Q_\nu[D(\nu_u\Vert\mu_u)],
                                                               \label{warm:spin-loss}\\
 Q_\nu\!\left[\frac{\mathcal E_{\mu_u}(f)}{N_u}\right]
       &=\frac1N Q_\mu[\mathcal E_{\mu_u}(f)]
       \le\frac{\mathcal E(f)}N .                                \label{warm:conditioned-energy}
\end{aligned}$$ The posterior $\nu_u$ is defined where $N_u>0$; the remaining observation paths have $Q_\nu$-mass zero and contribute zero to these averaged formulas. The loss identity has the corresponding stopped-path form, with the information in precision jumps added. The last inequality is conditional-variance contraction, site by site, under the ordinary joint spin-observation law. The form at every posterior uses the same rate-one-per-site normalization as $\mathcal E$.

<a id="stmt-warm-product"></a>
<div id="warm:product" class="lemma">

<a id="warm:product-bounds"></a>
**Lemma 18** (Product-posterior entropy bounds). *Fix the at most two product endpoints used below. Each has precision $t'I+W$ for a fixed $t'>3$, chosen from the fixed path parameters before $f$. On the common disorder event of (OpenAI 2026b, Equation (19.10)) <a id="pm-cite-59"></a>[[CM](#ref-CM)] for these endpoints, including its polynomial-moment field-tail control, the tests <a href="#warm:restricted-class" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="warm:restricted-class">[warm:restricted-class]</a> satisfy $$H_{\rm end}\le
 C\sqrt{\log n+L}\,\frac{\mathcal E(f)}N+O(n^{-3}),
 \qquad
 H_{\rm end}\le\frac{\mathcal I(f^2)}N .                         \label{warm:product-bounds}$$ The constants in the first inequality, including its remainder, may depend on these endpoints, the fixed path parameters, and $C_{\mathrm{lev}}$, but not on $n$ or $f$. The second inequality holds for every observation channel whose posterior at the endpoint is a product measure; it does not require a field-tail estimate.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-warm-product"><summary>Proof of stmt-warm-product</summary>

*Proof.* The first inequality is the product calculation of (OpenAI 2026b, Equation (19.18)) <a id="pm-cite-60"></a>[[CM](#ref-CM)], applied at each chosen endpoint. Its precision is $t'I+W$ for the corresponding fixed $t'>3$. The posterior interaction is then a scalar diagonal, hence its spin law is a product with fields $h_i$. Tensorizing the two-point log-Sobolev bound gives $$D(\nu_h\Vert\mu_h)
 \le C(1+\|h\|_\infty)\frac{\mathcal E_{\mu_h}(f)}{N_h}.$$ The field tail of (OpenAI 2026b, Equation (19.10)) <a id="pm-cite-61"></a>[[CM](#ref-CM)], on the common event for the chosen endpoints, restricts $\|h\|_\infty\le C\sqrt{\log n+L}$. Its ordinary complement has probability at most $e^{-2L}n^{-10}$, with polynomial moments; after the likelihood bound $N_h/N\le e^L$ its entropy contribution is $O(n^{-3})$. Equation <a href="#warm:conditioned-energy" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="warm:conditioned-energy">[warm:conditioned-energy]</a> gives the displayed bound.

For the second inequality, entropy tensorization at a product posterior and Jensen’s inequality for the logarithm give, for positive $z$, $$\mathop{\mathrm{Ent}}_{\mu_h}(z)
 \le\sum_i\mu_h[\mathop{\mathrm{Ent}}_{\mu_h(\cdot\mid X_{-i})}(z)]
 \le\sum_i\mu_h[\mathop{\mathrm{Cov}}_{\mu_h(\cdot\mid X_{-i})}(z,\log z)]
 =\mathcal I_{\mu_h}(z).$$ In fact $\mathop{\mathrm{Ent}}_\pi(z)\le\mathop{\mathrm{Cov}}_\pi(z,\log z)$ follows from $\pi[\log z]\le\log\pi[z]$. The posterior entropy formula is $$H_{\rm end}=\frac1N Q_\mu[\mathop{\mathrm{Ent}}_{\mu_h}(f^2)].$$ It remains to compare the averaged modified form to its initial value. For a fixed site and fixed $x_{-i}$, let $$a_h=\mu_h(X_{-i}=x_{-i},X_i=+1),\qquad
 b_h=\mu_h(X_{-i}=x_{-i},X_i=-1)$$ be the two joint posterior masses. Their contribution to $\mathcal I_{\mu_h}(z)$ is $$\frac{a_hb_h}{a_h+b_h}
       (z_+-z_-)(\log z_+-\log z_-).$$ The second factor is nonnegative and independent of the observation. The function $c(a,b)=ab/(a+b)$, extended by zero on the coordinate axes, is concave: in the positive quadrant its Hessian is $-2(b,-a)(b,-a)^{\mathsf T}/(a+b)^3$. Since $Q_\mu[a_h]$ and $Q_\mu[b_h]$ are the corresponding initial masses, Jensen’s inequality proves $Q_\mu[\mathcal I_{\mu_h}(z)]\le\mathcal I_\mu(z)$. Take $z=f^2+\epsilon$ and let $\epsilon\downarrow0$ to include zeros. This proves the second bound. ◻

</details>

At entropy of order $n$, the observation path must be stopped before its field leaves a region where the posterior mean is controlled. The following strengthening of the square-density estimate in (OpenAI 2026a, Proposition 7.3) <a id="pm-cite-62"></a>[[SG](#ref-SG)] is what permits the necessary energy range. We display the stability condition used at subcritical posterior interactions; the finite word estimates and vector recipes of (OpenAI 2026a) <a id="pm-cite-63"></a>[[SG](#ref-SG)] are used in their stated form.

<a id="warm:stability"></a>
Let $J_*=\beta W_{\rm off}$, $0<\beta<1$, and $j=\beta^2$. For $y,h\in\mathbb R^n$ put $$\begin{gathered}
 m(y)=\tanh y,\qquad q(y)=\frac{\|m(y)\|^2}{n},\qquad
 V(y)=\mathop{\mathrm{diag}}(1-m_i(y)^2),\\
 F_h(y)=y+\bigl(j(1-q(y))I-J_*\bigr)m(y)-h .
\end{gathered}$$ The stability condition of (OpenAI 2026b, Equation (17.2)) <a id="pm-cite-64"></a>[[CM](#ref-CM)], with fixed positive $b,\eta,\epsilon_A,\rho_0$, is the implication $$\begin{gathered}
 n^{-1/2}\|F_h(y)\|\le2\rho_0,\qquad 0\preceq A\preceq(1+\eta)I,\\
 A\ \hbox{diagonal},\qquad
 n^{-1/2}\|A-V(y)\|_{\rm F}\le\epsilon_A\\
\Longrightarrow\quad
 I+A^{1/2}\left(j(1-q(y))I-J_*
       -\frac{2j}{n}m(y)m(y)^{\mathsf T}\right)A^{1/2}\succeq bI .
\end{gathered}
                                                               \label{warm:stability}$$ for every $y,A$. The ordinary word diagnostics below are the simultaneous estimates of (OpenAI 2026a, Lemma 3.1) <a id="pm-cite-65"></a>[[SG](#ref-SG)]: for a prescribed finite length they bound the operator norm, the off-diagonal entrywise $\ell^4$ norm, and the Euclidean norm of the diagonal error from the noncrossing prediction for products of $J_*$ and bounded diagonal matrices. The ordinary vector recipes are those of (OpenAI 2026a, Definition 6.2) <a id="pm-cite-66"></a>[[SG](#ref-SG)]; their square-density argument uses no inverse word.

<a id="stmt-warm-posterior-mean"></a>
<div id="warm:posterior-mean" class="lemma">

<a id="warm:sqrt-posterior"></a>
**Lemma 19** (Square-root energy in a reweighted posterior mean). *Fix an operator-norm bound for $J_*$ and the parameters in <a href="#warm:stability" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="warm:stability">[warm:stability]</a>, with $j(1+\eta)^2<1$. For every sufficiently small fixed $\epsilon>0$, impose the ordinary word diagnostics of a finite length depending on $\epsilon$. For any field $h$ satisfying <a href="#warm:stability" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="warm:stability">[warm:stability]</a>, taking $A=V(y)$ verifies the hypothesis of (OpenAI 2026a, Lemma 5.7) <a id="pm-cite-67"></a>[[SG](#ref-SG)] with residual threshold $2\rho_0\sqrt n$ and lower bound $b$. Let $y_*$ be its unique root of $F_h$, and set $m_*=\tanh y_*$. This root existence is the source conclusion; the square-root energy dependence below is the new estimate. Define $$\mu_h(\sigma)\ \propto\
   \exp\{\tfrac12\sigma^{\mathsf T}J_*\sigma+h^{\mathsf T}\sigma\},
 \qquad
 \mathcal D_h(f):=\mathcal E_{\mu_h}(f)
       =\sum_i\mu_h[\mathop{\mathrm{Var}}(f\mid\sigma_{-i})].$$ For every real $f$ with $N_h=\mu_h[f^2]>0$ and $\nu_h=f^2\mu_h/N_h$, $$\frac{\|\nu_h[\sigma]-m_*\|}{\sqrt n}
 \le C_{\rm lead}\epsilon+
       \frac{C_\epsilon}{\sqrt n}
          \left(1+\sqrt{\frac{\mathcal D_h(f)}{N_h}}\right).
                                                               \label{warm:sqrt-posterior}$$ The constants are uniform in $n,h,f$ under these hypotheses. $C_{\rm lead}$ depends only on the fixed stability and norm bounds; the finite diagnostic length and $C_\epsilon$ may depend on $\epsilon$. The statement is simultaneous on a fixed compact subinterval of $(0,1)$ carrying a common strict margin, as in the last paragraph of the proof of (OpenAI 2026b, Proposition 17.1) <a id="pm-cite-68"></a>[[CM](#ref-CM)].*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-warm-posterior-mean"><summary>Proof of stmt-warm-posterior-mean</summary>

<a id="warm:sqrt-residual"></a>
*Proof.* We prove the stronger square-density residual estimate that replaces the linear energy dependence in (OpenAI 2026a, Lemma 6.5) <a id="pm-cite-69"></a>[[SG](#ref-SG)]. Use the zero-diagonal interaction $J_*$, so the cube coordinates in this proof are spins, not the scaled edge coordinates. For a spin flip $\sigma^{(i)}$, put $$d_i g(\sigma)=\frac{g(\sigma)-g(\sigma^{(i)})}{2\sigma_i}.$$ The primary iterates of (OpenAI 2026a, sec. 6) <a id="pm-cite-70"></a>[[SG](#ref-SG)] are $$\begin{gathered}
 m^0=\sigma,\qquad h^1=h+J_*\sigma,\qquad
 m^l=\tanh h^l,\qquad b_l=1-\|m^l\|^2/n,\\
 h^{l+1}=h+J_*m^l-jb_lm^{l-1},\qquad
 R_l=m^{l-1}-m^l .
\end{gathered}$$ For a fixed ordinary recipe admissible from level $l$, let $U$ be a terminal vector in that recipe. We claim that, whenever $\sup_\sigma(|H_0|+\|dH_0\|)\le C_0$, $$\left|\mu_h[f^2H_0R_l^{\mathsf T}U]\right|
 \le C\left(N_h+\sqrt{N_h\mathcal D_h(f)}\right).
                                                               \label{warm:sqrt-residual}$$ The constant has the dependence on the fixed recipe, depth, coefficient bounds and finite word diagnostics allowed in the source lemma, and is independent of $f$. The residual claim itself does not require root stability.

Here are the base case and the induction, including the point where the improvement occurs. The pointwise estimate (OpenAI 2026a, Lemma 6.4, Equation (6.20)) <a id="pm-cite-71"></a>[[SG](#ref-SG)] gives $$\|U\|+\sum_i|d_iU_i|\le C .$$ It also gives the same bound for $\widetilde U=H_0U$: indeed $$d_i(H_0U_i)=H_0\,d_iU_i+U_i(\sigma^{(i)})d_iH_0,
 \qquad
 \|(U_i(\sigma^{(i)}))_i\|
       \le\|U\|+2\|\mathop{\mathrm{diag}}\nabla U\|_2\le C,$$ and Cauchy–Schwarz bounds the sum of the added diagonal derivatives. Write $C_U$ for a bound on $\|\widetilde U\|+\sum_i|d_i\widetilde U_i|$.

Let $p_i^\pm=\mu_h(\sigma_i=\pm1\mid\sigma_{-i})$. Then $m_i^1=p_i^+-p_i^-$ and the conditional variance is $v_i^1=4p_i^+p_i^-$, in particular $v_i^1\le4p_i^\pm$ for each sign. Since a function of one spin is affine with slope $d_if$, the form is $$\mathcal D_h(f)=\mu_h\sum_i v_i^1(d_if)^2 .$$ The exact one-site integration by parts (OpenAI 2026a, Equation (6.31)) <a id="pm-cite-72"></a>[[SG](#ref-SG)] gives $$\begin{aligned}
 \mu_h[f^2R_1^{\mathsf T}\widetilde U]
 &=\mu_h\sum_i v_i^1d_i(f^2\widetilde U_i)\\
 &=\mu_h\sum_i v_i^1 f^2d_i\widetilde U_i
   +\mu_h\sum_i v_i^1(f_{i,+}+f_{i,-})d_if\,
                                  \widetilde U_i(\sigma^{(i)}).
\end{aligned}$$ Here $f_{i,\pm}=f(\sigma^{i,\pm})$, and $d_i(f^2)=(f_{i,+}+f_{i,-})d_if$, also for signed $f$. The first term is at most $C_UN_h$ in absolute value. For the second set $$M_i(\sigma_{-i})=\max_\pm|\widetilde U_i(\sigma^{i,\pm})|.$$ At each configuration, $$\left(\sum_iM_i(\sigma_{-i})^2\right)^{1/2}
 \le\|\widetilde U(\sigma)\|
       +2\|\mathop{\mathrm{diag}}\nabla\widetilde U(\sigma)\|_2\le 2C_U.$$ Weighted Cauchy–Schwarz bounds that second term by $$\mathcal D_h(f)^{1/2}
 \left(\mu_h\sum_i v_i^1(f_{i,+}+f_{i,-})^2M_i^2\right)^{1/2}.$$ The two separate bounds $v_i^1\le4p_i^\pm$ imply $$v_i^1(f_{i,+}+f_{i,-})^2
       \le8(p_i^+f_{i,+}^2+p_i^-f_{i,-}^2).$$ Since $M_i$ is independent of $\sigma_i$, conditioning term by term gives $$\mu_h\sum_i v_i^1(f_{i,+}+f_{i,-})^2M_i^2
       \le8\mu_h\!\left[f^2\sum_iM_i^2\right]\le32C_U^2N_h .$$ This proves <a href="#warm:sqrt-residual" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="warm:sqrt-residual">[warm:sqrt-residual]</a> for $l=1$.

The finite induction in the source preserves this new right side. For clarity, let $U$ be admissible from level $l+1$, put $a_l=j(b_l-b_{l-1})$, and define $$U_i'=\Phi(h_i^l;h_i^{l+1},a_l)U_i,\qquad
 \Phi(z;v,a)=\int_0^1
 e^{a(1-u^2)/2}\frac{\cosh(u(z-v))}{\cosh z\cosh v}\,\,\mathrm du .$$ Here $|a_l|\le j$. The integral formula bounds $\Phi$ and every needed fixed-order derivative uniformly in its two real field arguments: the hyperbolic derivatives introduce bounded hyperbolic-tangent factors, and the exponential factor and its derivatives are bounded for $|a|\le j$. Together with the explicit level indices, these bounds make $U'$ admissible from level $l$. The scalar identity in (OpenAI 2026a, sec. 6) <a id="pm-cite-73"></a>[[SG](#ref-SG)] then gives the residual expansion below. Adjoin the auxiliary field $$y'=J_*U'-j\sum_q\theta_qm^{q-1}
              -j\sum_b\omega_bw^b,\qquad
 \theta_q=\frac1n\sum_i\partial_qU'_i,\quad
 \omega_b=\frac1n\sum_i\partial_{y^b}U'_i .$$ Here $w^b,y^b$ are the finitely many earlier auxiliary sources and fields of the recipe; the partials differentiate their explicitly displayed local arguments, holding parameters fixed, as in (OpenAI 2026a, Definition 6.2) <a id="pm-cite-74"></a>[[SG](#ref-SG)]. Equation (6.33) of that source is $$\begin{aligned}
 R_{l+1}^{\mathsf T}U
 ={}&R_l^{\mathsf T}y'+a_lR_l^{\mathsf T}U'
       -jb_{l-1}R_{l-1}^{\mathsf T}U'
       +j\sum_b\omega_bR_l^{\mathsf T}w^b\\
 &+j\sum_{q\ge l}\theta_qR_l^{\mathsf T}m^{q-1}
       -a_ln\theta_l ,
\end{aligned}$$ with the $R_{l-1}$ term absent when $l=1$. All first-line terms are earlier residuals with ordinary admissible sources. Their scalar multipliers and their discrete-gradient norms are bounded by the fixed-recipe bounds. For $q>l$ in the second line, use the source $m^{q-1}/\sqrt n$ and multiplier $j\sqrt n\,\theta_q$; (OpenAI 2026a, Equation (6.21)) gives the same boundedness for that multiplier. Finally the exact identity $$R_l^{\mathsf T}m^{l-1}
       =n(b_l-b_{l-1})-R_l^{\mathsf T}m^l$$ cancels the displayed $-a_ln\theta_l$. The remainder again uses an earlier residual, the source $m^l/\sqrt n$, and a bounded multiplier. A bounded multiplier $\zeta$ with bounded $\|d\zeta\|$ can always be absorbed into $H_0$, because $$d_i(\zeta H_0)=\zeta(\sigma^{(i)})d_iH_0+H_0(\sigma)d_i\zeta .$$ Every induction call therefore retains the original $f,N_h,\mathcal D_h(f)$. There are finitely many calls with a smaller residual index. This proves <a href="#warm:sqrt-residual" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="warm:sqrt-residual">[warm:sqrt-residual]</a> at every fixed depth.

<a id="warm:sqrt-selection-moment"></a>
We spell out its consequences for selection and the mean. Put $S_l=R_l^{\mathsf T}m^l/\sqrt n$. The primary derivative bounds in (OpenAI 2026a, Lemma 7.1) <a id="pm-cite-75"></a>[[SG](#ref-SG)] give $|S_l|\le2\sqrt n$ and $\|dS_l\|\le C_l$. Apply <a href="#warm:sqrt-residual" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="warm:sqrt-residual">[warm:sqrt-residual]</a> with $U=m^l/\sqrt n$ and $H_0=S_l/\sqrt n$. Division by $N_h\sqrt n$ yields the strengthened form of (OpenAI 2026a, Equation (7.1)) <a id="pm-cite-76"></a>[[SG](#ref-SG)]: $$\nu_h\!\left[\left(\frac{S_l}{\sqrt n}\right)^2\right]
 \le\frac{C_l}{\sqrt n}
       \left(1+\sqrt{\frac{\mathcal D_h(f)}{N_h}}\right).
                                                               \label{warm:sqrt-selection-moment}$$ For a small fixed $\rho>0$, choose a fixed depth $d$ with $\lfloor d/2\rfloor\rho^2/4>2$, and then $e_\rho>0$ with $2de_\rho<1$. The telescoping identity $$\frac{\|R_l\|^2}{n}=b_l-b_{l-1}-\frac{2S_l}{\sqrt n}$$ shows that $\max_{l\le d}|S_l|/\sqrt n\le e_\rho$ forces a consecutive pair $R_{k-1},R_k$ to have both norms at most $\rho\sqrt n/2$. Otherwise the disjoint pairs would make the sum of squared norms exceed $2$, whereas telescoping bounds it by $1+2de_\rho<2$.

<a id="warm:sqrt-deficit"></a>
As in that source lemma, choose smooth $C_k\in[0,1]$, equal to one on this smaller pair region and supported where both norms are at most $\rho\sqrt n$. The primary derivative bounds give $\|dC_k\|\le C_\rho/\sqrt n$. Put $$\widehat C_k=C_k\prod_{i=2}^{k-1}(1-C_i),\qquad
 D_{\rm sel}=1-\sum_{k=2}^d\widehat C_k=\prod_{k=2}^d(1-C_k).$$ Positive deficit implies $\max_{l\le d}|S_l|/\sqrt n>e_\rho$. Chebyshev’s inequality and <a href="#warm:sqrt-selection-moment" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="warm:sqrt-selection-moment">[warm:sqrt-selection-moment]</a> give $$\nu_h(D_{\rm sel}>0)
 \le\frac{C_\rho}{\sqrt n}
       \left(1+\sqrt{\frac{\mathcal D_h(f)}{N_h}}\right).
                                                               \label{warm:sqrt-deficit}$$ The cutoffs are admissible bounded multipliers in <a href="#warm:sqrt-residual" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="warm:sqrt-residual">[warm:sqrt-residual]</a>.

Choose $\rho\le\epsilon$ with $(\|J_*\|+4j)\rho<2\rho_0$. On the support of $C_k$, the recursion gives $$F_h(h^k)=J_*R_k-jb_{k-1}(R_{k-1}+R_k)
                  +j(b_k-b_{k-1})m^k,$$ so $\|F_h(h^k)\|\le(\|J_*\|+4j)\rho\sqrt n$. The root estimate of (OpenAI 2026a, Lemma 5.7) <a id="pm-cite-77"></a>[[SG](#ref-SG)], $$\|y-y_*\|\le
 \left(1+\frac{\|J_*\|+3j}{b}\right)\|F_h(y)\|
 \quad\hbox{when }\|F_h(y)\|<2\rho_0\sqrt n,$$ and the Lipschitz property of $\tanh$ therefore give $\|m^k-m_*\|\le C_{\rm lead}\rho\sqrt n$, with a constant independent of the depth. For a deterministic unit vector $e$, sum <a href="#warm:sqrt-residual" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="warm:sqrt-residual">[warm:sqrt-residual]</a> for $R_1,\ldots,R_k$, with source $e$ and multiplier $\widehat C_k$. Since $\sigma-m^k=\sum_{l\le k}R_l$, this bounds its reweighted mean against $e$ by $C_\rho(1+\sqrt{\mathcal D_h(f)/N_h})$. The weighted root errors together cost at most $C_{\rm lead}\epsilon\sqrt n$, because the cutoffs sum to at most one. The remaining deficit costs at most $2\sqrt n\,\nu_h(D_{\rm sel}>0)$, controlled by <a href="#warm:sqrt-deficit" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="warm:sqrt-deficit">[warm:sqrt-deficit]</a>. Sum over the fixed number of cutoffs, divide by $\sqrt n$, and take the supremum over $e$. This proves <a href="#warm:sqrt-posterior" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="warm:sqrt-posterior">[warm:sqrt-posterior]</a>. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-warm-large-retention"></a>
<div id="warm:large-retention" class="lemma">

<a id="warm:large-energy-assumption"></a>
**Lemma 20** (Retention at order-$n$ entropy). *Fix $0<\lambda<C_{\mathrm{lev}}<\infty$, $C_E<\infty$, and $0<\omega<1$. On Gaussian disorder events of probability tending to one, every test <a href="#warm:restricted-class" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="warm:restricted-class">[warm:restricted-class]</a> with $\lambda n\le L\le C_{\mathrm{lev}}n$ and $$\frac{\mathcal E(f)}N\le C_E n^{1-\omega}                       \label{warm:large-energy-assumption}$$ has an observation path to a product posterior for which $H_{\rm end}\ge c_{\lambda,C_{\mathrm{lev}}}n$. The path and disorder events are chosen independently of $f$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-warm-large-retention"><summary>Proof of stmt-warm-large-retention</summary>

*Proof.* We use the path and the field tests in (OpenAI 2026b, sec. 19.6) <a id="pm-cite-78"></a>[[CM](#ref-CM)]; we verify that its entropy argument remains valid under <a href="#warm:large-energy-assumption" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="warm:large-energy-assumption">[warm:large-energy-assumption]</a>. On source disorder events independent of the initial spin law, the calculation around Equation (19.20) there, using its Lemma 17.4, Equation (17.12), and Proposition 17.5, gives the following early field-test bound. On a fixed interval $[t_*,t_b]$ of small positive scalar precision, the diagnostic and stability failures have integrated probability $o(1)$, uniformly under every initial spin law. This follows there by conditioning on the spin: the centered Gaussian-noise diagnostics have integrated failure $o(1)$, the additional spin shift has normalized norm $O(t)$, and the Gaussian low-band small-ball estimate is uniform in its center. No factor $e^L$ is used for this interval. From $t_b$ until the interaction coefficient reaches a fixed globally controlled range, the buffered stability test fails anywhere on the path with probability at most $e^{-a n}$ under the ordinary law $Q_\mu$, for a fixed $a>0$. This is the later field bound in (OpenAI 2026b, Lemma 17.3, Section 19.4, and Section 19.6 after Equation (19.21)) <a id="pm-cite-79"></a>[[CM](#ref-CM)]. The word diagnostics and stability constants on the retained regions are those of Lemma <a href="#warm:posterior-mean" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="warm:posterior-mean">19</a>.

Here is the order of the fixed choices in that construction. Choose first a large scalar endpoint $t_{\rm end}$ and a small interaction coefficient below which covariance is globally bounded. Choose $t_b>0$ for the small-positive-field estimate, and obtain the buffer and rate $a$ for the later test. The norm bound and the fixed total duration give constants $C_{\rm jump}$ and $C_{\rm aft}$ for the jump loss divided by $t_*n$ and the loss after failure divided by $n$, uniformly when $1-\beta'\le t_*/3$. Choose a target drift budget $\eta_1>0$ so that $$3\eta_1(1+C_{\rm aft}/a)<\lambda/4.$$ Next choose $0<t_*\ll t_b$ with $C_{\rm jump}t_*\le\eta_1$, and finally $1-\beta'>0$ sufficiently small relative to these choices, including $1-\beta'\le t_*/3$. Start with precision $$B_*=t_*I+(1-\beta')W,$$ which is positive when $1-\beta'$ is small enough. Increase scalar precision to $t_{\rm end}I+(1-\beta')W$, and then traverse $$B_v=(t_{\rm end}+4v)I+(1-\beta'+v)W,\qquad 0\le v\le\beta'.$$ The latter rate $4I+W$ is positive on the norm event. The endpoint is $(t_{\rm end}+4\beta')I+W$, so its posterior is a product. Before the globally controlled portion, the posterior interaction coefficient is either $\beta'<1$ or in a fixed compact subinterval of $(0,1)$. Reduce the available diagonal enlargement in <a href="#warm:stability" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="warm:stability">[warm:stability]</a> to $0<\eta<(\beta')^{-1}-1$. Once these stability margins and $C_{\rm lead}$ are fixed, choose the mean accuracy $\epsilon$ in Lemma <a href="#warm:posterior-mean" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="warm:posterior-mean">19</a> so that its leading error, integrated over the bounded path and converted to a quadratic mean bound, is less than $\eta_1$. Then fix its residual tolerance, selection depth, finite word diagnostics and constant $C_\epsilon$, and finally take $n$ large.

On a valid posterior, apply <a href="#warm:sqrt-posterior" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="warm:sqrt-posterior">[warm:sqrt-posterior]</a> to $f$ and to $1$. With $a_u=\|\nu_u[X]-\mu_u[X]\|/\sqrt n$, this gives $$a_u\le2C_{\rm lead}\epsilon+
       \frac{C_\epsilon}{\sqrt n}
          \left(2+\sqrt{\frac{\mathcal E_{\mu_u}(f)}{N_u}}\right).$$ By <a href="#warm:conditioned-energy" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="warm:conditioned-energy">[warm:conditioned-energy]</a> and Cauchy–Schwarz, the $Q_\nu$-mean of the square root, also with any validity indicator, is at most $\sqrt{\mathcal E(f)/N}$. Under <a href="#warm:large-energy-assumption" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="warm:large-energy-assumption">[warm:large-energy-assumption]</a> the resulting error is $$\frac{C_\epsilon}{\sqrt n}
       \left(2+\sqrt{\frac{\mathcal E(f)}N}\right)
       =O_\epsilon(n^{-1/2}+n^{-\omega/2})=o(1).$$ This bound is applied at deterministic observation times; inserting $\mathbf 1_{\{u<\tau\}}$ for a stopping time only decreases its Cauchy–Schwarz bound. Since $a_u\le2$ always, $a_u^2\le2a_u$. The early invalid paths cost at most four times their integrated probability, hence $o(1)$. Thus the normalized quadratic mean-shift integral, on valid paths and before any later stopping, is at most $\eta_1+o(1)$ by the preceding choice of $\epsilon$.

Let $u_g$ begin the globally controlled portion and let $\tau$ be the first failure of the later buffered test in $[t_b,u_g]$, with the immediate and no-failure conventions of the source. The initial jump leaks at most $C_{\rm jump}t_*n$ entropy: compare to pure noise as above and use $\|B_*\|\le Ct_*$ and $\|X\|^2=n$. The stopped form of <a href="#warm:spin-loss" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="warm:spin-loss">[warm:spin-loss]</a>, with the preceding integrated estimate, gives, with $Q^\tau$ denoting the law of the stopped observations, excluding the spin, <a id="warm:stopped-entropy"></a>$$D(Q_\nu^\tau\Vert Q_\mu^\tau)
       \le(C_{\rm jump}t_*+\eta_1+o(1))n .              \label{warm:stopped-entropy}$$ For the event $E$ of a failure before $u_g$, the ordinary probability is at most $e^{-an}$. Data processing for its indicator then gives $$D(Q_\nu^\tau\Vert Q_\mu^\tau)
 \ge Q_\nu(E)\log\frac1{Q_\mu(E)}-\log2,\qquad
 Q_\nu(E)\le\frac{C_{\rm jump}t_*+\eta_1+o(1)}a .$$ These are exactly the deductions in (OpenAI 2026b, Equations (19.21)–(19.22)) <a id="pm-cite-80"></a>[[CM](#ref-CM)], now with the enlarged energy range justified by Lemma <a href="#warm:posterior-mean" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="warm:posterior-mean">19</a>. After a failure the remaining precision rate and duration are bounded, and both spin means have norm at most $\sqrt n$; the remaining loss per failed path is therefore at most $C_{\rm aft}n$. The total loss before $u_g$ is bounded by $$\left(C_{\rm jump}t_*+\eta_1+o(1)\right)
       (1+C_{\rm aft}/a)n .$$ The fixed choices above make this less than $\lambda n/4$. The initial entropy is at least $L/2\ge\lambda n/2$, hence $H(u_g)\ge\lambda n/4$. In the remaining portion the spin covariance is bounded for every field. The linear entropy test then gives $-\dot H\le CH$; over its bounded duration it retains a fixed fraction of $H(u_g)$. This proves the lemma. ◻

</details>

<details id="proof-stmt-warm-large-retention-2"><summary>Proof of stmt-warm-large-retention</summary>

*Proof of Proposition <a href="#warm:profiles" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="warm:profiles">16</a>.* Fix $C_{\mathrm{lev}},\xi$ and a desired disorder confidence. Apply Lemma <a href="#warm:small-profile" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="warm:small-profile">17</a> with $\kappa<\min\{\xi,\,5/3-1.662\}$. After fixing its $M$, choose its $\delta>0$ as in that proof. For $L\le n^\delta$, <a href="#warm:small-profile-bound" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="warm:small-profile-bound">[warm:small-profile-bound]</a> and <a href="#warm:modified-classical" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="warm:modified-classical">[warm:modified-classical]</a> imply both claimed inequalities.

<a id="warm:moderate-retention"></a>
For $n^\delta<L\le\lambda n$, use the proportional branch of (OpenAI 2026b, Equation (19.16) and Section 19.4) <a id="pm-cite-81"></a>[[CM](#ref-CM)]. It gives, at the product endpoint, $$H_{\rm end}\ge cL(L/n)^{(2+2\epsilon)/3}.                \label{warm:moderate-retention}$$ Here $\epsilon>0$ is any fixed sufficiently small tolerance, and $\lambda>0$ is chosen afterward. We justify the exact test class being used. The starting dimension in that source is $\max\{k_{\min},c_0L\}$, with $k_{\min}\asymp\sqrt{\log n}$. It equals $c_0L$ throughout the present range for large $n$. The proportional part of its initial jump estimate is the pure-noise argument reproduced in Lemma <a href="#warm:small-profile" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="warm:small-profile">17</a>; it requires only the entropy at least $L/2$ and density at most $e^L$. The source’s support condition is used in its other, minimum-dimension branch. Its subsequent propagation uses the likelihood and conditional-entropy tails in (OpenAI 2026b, Equation (19.8)) <a id="pm-cite-82"></a>[[CM](#ref-CM)] and the ordinary path tests. These also require only the same density and entropy bounds. The continuation through its finite remaining scales uses those likelihood tails and conditional Pinsker bounds, then globally bounded covariance, and so preserves this test class. Thus <a href="#warm:moderate-retention" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="warm:moderate-retention">[warm:moderate-retention]</a> applies to <a href="#warm:restricted-class" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="warm:restricted-class">[warm:restricted-class]</a> without a support restriction.

Since $L\ge n^\delta\gg\log n$, comparison with the first bound of <a href="#warm:product-bounds" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="warm:product-bounds">[warm:product-bounds]</a> gives $$T_n\,\frac{\mathcal E(f)}N
 \ge c n^{-2\epsilon/3}L^{7/6+2\epsilon/3}
 \ge c L^{7/6-(2\epsilon/3)(1/\delta-1)}.$$ The additive $O(n^{-3})$ is smaller than <a href="#warm:moderate-retention" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="warm:moderate-retention">[warm:moderate-retention]</a>. The second product bound similarly gives $$T_n\,\frac{\mathcal I(f^2)}N
 \ge c n^{-2\epsilon/3}L^{5/3+2\epsilon/3}
 \ge c L^{5/3-(2\epsilon/3)(1/\delta-1)}.$$ Choose $\epsilon$ after $\delta$ so that $$\frac{2\epsilon}{3}(1/\delta-1)
       <\min\{\xi,\,7/6-1.162\}.$$ Then choose $\lambda$ below the finitely many fixed rates and shift buffers in that source argument. This proves the profiles in the moderate range.

Finally let $\lambda n\le L\le C_{\mathrm{lev}}n$. If the classical bound were false, then $\mathcal E(f)/N\le Cn^{1.162-2/3}$. This meets <a href="#warm:large-energy-assumption" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="warm:large-energy-assumption">[warm:large-energy-assumption]</a> for a fixed positive $\omega$, whereas the first product bound would give $$H_{\rm end}\le Cn^{1/2+1.162-2/3}+O(n^{-3})=o(n),$$ contrary to Lemma <a href="#warm:large-retention" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="warm:large-retention">20</a>. If the modified bound were false, <a href="#warm:modified-classical" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="warm:modified-classical">[warm:modified-classical]</a> would instead give $\mathcal E(f)/N\le Cn^{1-\xi}$, so that lemma applies with $\omega=\xi$. The second product bound would give $H_{\rm end}\le Cn^{1-\xi}=o(n)$, again a contradiction.

All the choices are uniform in $f$. More explicitly, the variance exponent and $M$ are fixed first, then the small $\delta$, then the sharp cap and moderate-entropy tolerances, then $\lambda$ and the fixed parameters of the order-$n$ path. The finite word length in that last path is fixed after its mean accuracy. The final threshold $K_0$ and $n$ are chosen last. Intersecting this finite collection of disorder events preserves arbitrarily high limiting probability. This proves the proposition. ◻

</details>

<a id="warm:layers-section"></a>
#### Passage from profiles to arbitrary initial laws

<a id="warm:atom"></a>
On the norm event $\|W\|\le3$, comparison of the largest and smallest spin Hamiltonians gives $$\min_\sigma\mu(\sigma)\ge e^{-C_a n}                     \label{warm:atom}$$ for an absolute $C_a$. In the remainder of the proof choose $C_{\mathrm{lev}}>2C_a+1$ in Proposition <a href="#warm:profiles" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="warm:profiles">16</a>. For any density $z\ge0$, $\mu[z]=1$ implies $z(\sigma)\le1/\mu(\sigma)$; thus every nonempty positive logarithmic level of $z$ lies below $C_a n$.

We first isolate the bounded test associated with one such level. This same construction will be used for entropy and higher log moments.

<a id="stmt-warm-log-layer"></a>
<div id="warm:log-layer" class="lemma">

<a id="warm:level-dissipation"></a>
**Lemma 21** (A bounded test from a logarithmic level). *Fix $b>0$ and $r>0$. Let $z>0$ be a density and suppose that, for some $d\ge v/2$ and sufficiently large $v$, $$B=\mu[z\mathbf 1_{\{d\le\log z\le1.1d\}}]
       \ge b(v/d)^r>0 .$$ Define <a id="warm:level-transform"></a>$$u=\mathcal U_d(z)
   :=\min\{e^{1.1d},\,z\min(1,ze^{-0.8d})\},
 \qquad f^2=e^{-1.1d}u .                                 \label{warm:level-transform}$$ Then $0\le f\le1$, $B\le\mu[u]\le1$, and, if $N=\mu[f^2]=e^{-L}$, $$1.1d\le L\le1.1d+C_{b,r}\bigl(1+\log_+(d/v)\bigr),
 \qquad
 D\!\left(\frac{f^2\mu}{N}\middle\Vert\mu\right)\ge L/2 .$$ For large $v,n$, this test lies in the range $K_0\le L\le C_{\mathrm{lev}}n$ of Proposition <a href="#warm:profiles" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="warm:profiles">16</a>. In addition, $$\mathcal I(\mathcal U_d(z))\le4\mathcal I(z).                          \label{warm:level-dissipation}$$*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-warm-log-layer"><summary>Proof of stmt-warm-log-layer</summary>

*Proof.* In logarithmic coordinates $l=\log z$, the logarithm of $\mathcal U_d(e^l)$ is $$2l-0.8d\quad(l\le0.8d),\qquad
 l\quad(0.8d\le l\le1.1d),\qquad
 1.1d\quad(l\ge1.1d).$$ Consequently $u\le z$, and $u=z$ on the indicated level. This proves $B\le\mu[u]\le1$ and $L=1.1d-\log\mu[u]$, with the stated upper bound from the lower bound on $B$.

Let $E=\{\log z\ge0.7d\}$. Since $u\le e^{-0.1d}z$ on its complement, $$\frac{\mu[u\mathbf 1_{E^c}]}{\mu[u]}\le\frac{e^{-0.1d}}B,
 \qquad \mu(E)\le e^{-0.7d}.$$ Set $e_d=e^{-0.1d}/B$. Data processing for the indicator of $E$ gives $$D\!\left(\frac{u\mu}{\mu[u]}\middle\Vert\mu\right)
 \ge (1-e_d)\log\frac1{\mu(E)}-\log2
 \ge0.7d(1-e_d)-\log2 .$$ Uniformly for $d\ge v/2$, the hypothesis on $B$ makes $e_d\to0$ and $1+\log_+(d/v)=o(d)$ as $v\to\infty$. The last lower bound therefore exceeds $L/2$ for large $v$. The level is nonempty, so $d\le C_an$ by <a href="#warm:atom" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="warm:atom">[warm:atom]</a>; the bound on $L$, with $C_{\mathrm{lev}}>2C_a+1$, puts it below $C_{\mathrm{lev}}n$ for large $n$. Its lower bound puts it above $K_0$ for large $v$.

Finally $\mathcal U_d$ is nondecreasing and $2$-Lipschitz as a function of $z$, while $\log\mathcal U_d(e^l)$ is nondecreasing and $2$-Lipschitz as a function of $l$. The product of their increments on an edge is at most four times the product of the increments of $z$ and $\log z$. Summing proves <a href="#warm:level-dissipation" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="warm:level-dissipation">[warm:level-dissipation]</a>. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-warm-entropy-profile"></a>
<div id="warm:entropy-profile" class="lemma">

**Lemma 22** (Entropy dissipation for every density). *With tight constants, every strictly positive density $z$ with $\mathop{\mathrm{Ent}}_\mu(z)\ge K_1$ satisfies <a id="warm:full-entropy-profile"></a>$$T_n\mathcal I(z)\ge c\,\mathop{\mathrm{Ent}}_\mu(z)^{1.662}.                    \label{warm:full-entropy-profile}$$*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-warm-entropy-profile"><summary>Proof of stmt-warm-entropy-profile</summary>

*Proof.* Put $H=\mathop{\mathrm{Ent}}_\mu(z)$ and $d_j=(H/2)(1.1)^j$. The part of $\mu[z\log z]$ with $\log z<H/2$ is at most $H/2$. Thus the levels $[d_j,1.1d_j]$ account for at least $H/2$. If their tilted masses $B_j$ were all less than $c(H/d_j)^{1.1}$, their contribution would be at most $$1.1\sum_{j\ge0}d_jB_j
 <1.1cH^{1.1}\sum_{j\ge0}d_j^{-0.1}\le CcH .$$ Choose $c$ small. One level therefore has $B\ge c(H/d)^{1.1}$. Apply Lemma <a href="#warm:log-layer" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="warm:log-layer">21</a> with $v=H$ and $r=1.1$, followed by <a href="#warm:modified-profile" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="warm:modified-profile">[warm:modified-profile]</a> with any fixed $\xi<5/3-1.662$. Homogeneity of $\mathcal I$ gives $$T_n\mathcal I(z)\ge\tfrac14T_n\mathcal I(u)
       \ge c\,\mu[u]L^{1.662}
       \ge cB d^{1.662}
       \ge c'H^{1.1}d^{0.562}\ge c''H^{1.662}.$$ The constants and the required lower threshold on $H$ are uniform. ◻

</details>

For the kernel we need a classical support profile. The next deduction is the equal-height and dyadic-layer argument of (OpenAI 2026b, Lemma 19.1) <a id="pm-cite-83"></a>[[CM](#ref-CM)], keeping the two powers from <a href="#warm:classical-profile" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="warm:classical-profile">[warm:classical-profile]</a>.

<a id="stmt-warm-support-profile"></a>
<div id="warm:support-profile" class="lemma">

<a id="warm:support-bound"></a>
**Lemma 23** (A support profile). *With the constants and $\delta$ of Proposition <a href="#warm:profiles" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="warm:profiles">16</a>, every nonnegative $g$, supported on a set of $\mu$-mass $e^{-L_{\rm supp}}$ with $L_{\rm supp}\ge K_0$, satisfies $$T_n\mathcal E(g)\ge c\mu[g^2]\,\Phi_n(L_{\rm supp}),\qquad
 \Phi_n(L)=
 \begin{cases}
 \min\{L^{1.654},\,n^{1.154\delta}\},&L\le n^\delta,\\
 L^{1.154},&L>n^\delta .
 \end{cases}                                                \label{warm:support-bound}$$ The zero function satisfies the assertion by convention.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-warm-support-profile"><summary>Proof of stmt-warm-support-profile</summary>

<a id="warm:set-capacity"></a>
*Proof.* First let $0\le g\le1$ equal one on a nonempty set of mass $a=e^{-L_a}$, and let its support have mass at most $e^{-L_{\rm supp}}$. Take $$K=\left\lceil\log_2(1+L_a/L_{\rm supp})\right\rceil,\qquad
 g_i=K\bigl((g-i/K)_+\wedge K^{-1}\bigr),\quad 0\le i<K .$$ Let $S_i=\mu(g>i/K)$, $T_i=\mu(g\ge i/K)$. Some $i$ satisfies $T_{i+1}\ge S_i^2$; otherwise induction gives $a\le T_K<e^{-2^KL_{\rm supp}}<a$. For this $i$, with $N_i=\mu[g_i^2]$, $$a\le T_{i+1}\le N_i\le S_i,\qquad
 D\!\left(\frac{g_i^2\mu}{N_i}\middle\Vert\mu\right)
       \ge\log(1/S_i)\ge\tfrac12\log(1/N_i).$$ Its logarithmic inverse mass $L_i$ lies in $[L_{\rm supp},L_a]$, and $L_a\le C_an$ by <a href="#warm:atom" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="warm:atom">[warm:atom]</a>. For $L\ge K_0$ large enough, the function $$e^{-L}
 \begin{cases}L^{1.662},&L\le n^\delta,\\
               L^{1.162},&L>n^\delta
 \end{cases}$$ is decreasing within each range and has a downward jump at their boundary. Since $\mathcal E(g_i)\le K^2\mathcal E(g)$, <a href="#warm:classical-profile" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="warm:classical-profile">[warm:classical-profile]</a> implies $$T_n\mathcal E(g)\ge
 \frac{ca}{(1+\log L_a)^2}
 \begin{cases}L_a^{1.662},&L_a\le n^\delta,\\
               L_a^{1.162},&L_a>n^\delta .
 \end{cases}$$ Absorbing the logarithmic denominator by lowering each exponent by $0.008$ gives $$T_n\mathcal E(g)\ge ca
 \begin{cases}L_a^{1.654},&L_a\le n^\delta,\\
               L_a^{1.154},&L_a>n^\delta .
 \end{cases}                                                \label{warm:set-capacity}$$ Indeed $L^{0.008}/(1+\log L)^2$ has a positive infimum for $L\ge K_0$.

For arbitrary nonnegative $g$ with the stated support, use $\varphi_j=(g-2^j)_+\wedge2^j$, $j\in\mathbb Z$, and let $a_{j+1}=\mu(g\ge2^{j+1})$. Omit empty upper level sets. The normalized layer $2^{-j}\varphi_j$ is one on that set and has the original support restriction. Its $L_a=\log(1/a_{j+1})$ is at least $L_{\rm supp}$. The right side of <a href="#warm:set-capacity" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="warm:set-capacity">[warm:set-capacity]</a>, divided by $a$, is at least $\Phi_n(L_{\rm supp})$: before the boundary it is at least $L_{\rm supp}^{1.654}$, and after the boundary it is at least $n^{1.154\delta}$, or at least $L_{\rm supp}^{1.154}$ when $L_{\rm supp}>n^\delta$. For each oriented edge the nonnegative increments of the $\varphi_j$’s sum to the increment of $g$, so the sum of their squares is at most its square. Therefore $$T_n\mathcal E(g)\ge\sum_jT_n\mathcal E(\varphi_j)
       \ge c\Phi_n(L_{\rm supp})\sum_j4^ja_{j+1}.$$ Pointwise, $\sum_j4^j\mathbf 1_{\{g\ge2^{j+1}\}}\ge g^2/12$. Integration proves <a href="#warm:support-bound" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="warm:support-bound">[warm:support-bound]</a>. ◻

</details>

<details id="proof-stmt-warm-support-profile-2"><summary>Proof of stmt-warm-support-profile</summary>

*Proof of Theorem <a href="#thm:warming" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:warming">15</a>.* Fix the parameters in the theorem and intersect the finitely many events needed for the preceding results. The finite heat-bath chain has a strictly positive kernel at every positive time. Hence $w_s^\rho>0$ for $s>0$, for every initial law, and symmetry of the generator gives $$\frac{\,\mathrm d}{\,\mathrm ds}\mathop{\mathrm{Ent}}_\mu(w_s^\rho)
       =-T_n\mathcal I(w_s^\rho).$$ When the entropy exceeds the threshold of Lemma <a href="#warm:entropy-profile" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="warm:entropy-profile">22</a>, its derivative is at most $-c\mathop{\mathrm{Ent}}_\mu(w_s^\rho)^{1.662}$. Integrating this differential inequality from any earlier positive time, and then letting that time decrease to zero, yields uniformly in the initial law $$\mathop{\mathrm{Ent}}_\mu(w_s^\rho)
       \le C\left(1+s^{-1/0.662}\right)
       \le C'\left(1+s^{-1.54}\right).$$ This proves <a href="#warm:entropy" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="warm:entropy">[warm:entropy]</a>.

<a id="warm:hitting-integral"></a>
For the kernel, put $Q_s=\mu[(w_s^\rho)^2]=e^{L_s}$. The atom bound gives $Q_s\le e^{C_an}$, so its logarithm is within the range where the support profile was proved. Whenever $L_s$ is large, set $g=(w_s^\rho-Q_s/4)_+$. Its support has mass at most $4e^{-L_s}$ by $\mu[w_s^\rho]=1$, and $$\mu[g^2]\ge Q_s-2(Q_s/4)\mu[w_s^\rho]=Q_s/2,\qquad
 \mathcal E(g)\le\mathcal E(w_s^\rho).$$ Its actual support logarithm is $$L_{\rm supp}=\log\frac1{\mu\{w_s^\rho>Q_s/4\}}
       \ge L_s-\log4.$$ The support is nonempty by the preceding square-mass bound, so <a href="#warm:atom" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="warm:atom">[warm:atom]</a> also gives $L_{\rm supp}\le C_an$. Since $\dot Q_s=-2T_n\mathcal E(w_s^\rho)$, Lemma <a href="#warm:support-profile" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="warm:support-profile">23</a> and monotonicity of $\Phi_n$ give $$-\dot L_s\ge c\,\Phi_n(L_s-\log4)$$ above a fixed threshold. A shift of the argument by $\log4$ only changes constants there. For any large $K'$, the time allowed by this differential inequality above $K'$ is at most $$\int_{K'}^\infty\frac{C\,\,\mathrm dL}{\Phi_n(L)}
       \le C(K')^{-0.654}+C n^{-0.154\delta}.
                                                               \label{warm:hitting-integral}$$ For completeness, below $n^{\delta(1.154/1.654)}$ integrate $L^{-1.654}$. The following constant portion of $\Phi_n$, up to $n^\delta$, costs at most $n^\delta/n^{1.154\delta}$, and the integral of $L^{-1.154}$ above $n^\delta$ has the same order. Inverting <a href="#warm:hitting-integral" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="warm:hitting-integral">[warm:hitting-integral]</a> gives $$L_s\le C(1+s^{-1/0.654})
       \qquad\hbox{for }s\ge Cn^{-0.154\delta},$$ uniformly even for point initial laws. Reversibility and two half steps show that $$p_{sT_n}(\sigma,\tau)
 =\mu[p_{sT_n/2}(\sigma,\cdot)p_{sT_n/2}(\tau,\cdot)]
 \le\bigl(\mu[p_{sT_n/2}(\sigma,\cdot)^2]\,
          \mu[p_{sT_n/2}(\tau,\cdot)^2]\bigr)^{1/2}.$$ The preceding bound, with $1/0.654<1.54$, proves <a href="#warm:kernel" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="warm:kernel">[warm:kernel]</a> after enlarging the vanishing threshold.

<a id="warm:moment-comparison"></a>
We finish by proving <a href="#warm:log-moment" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="warm:log-moment">[warm:log-moment]</a>. For the fixed integer $m\ge1$, let $\Psi_m$ be the convex function on $(0,\infty)$ determined by $$\Psi_m(1)=\Psi_m'(1)=0,\qquad
 \Psi_m''(z)=\frac{(1+|\log z|)^{m-1}}{z}.$$ It extends continuously to zero: in its twice-integrated formula the possible singularity is bounded by $\int_0^1(1+|\log z|)^{m-1}\,\mathrm dz<\infty$. For a density $z$, put $$V_m(z)=\mu[\Psi_m(z)],\qquad
 \mathsf M_m(z)=\left(1+\mu[z(\log_+z)^m]\right)^{1/m}.$$ There are constants depending only on $m$ such that $$c_m\mathsf M_m(z)^m-C_m
       \le V_m(z)\le C_m\mathsf M_m(z)^m.                 \label{warm:moment-comparison}$$ Indeed for $z\ge1$, $\Psi_m'(z)=((1+\log z)^m-1)/m$. Integrating this on $[1,z]$ gives upper and lower bounds of order $z(\log z)^m$ when $\log z$ is large; the remaining range contributes at most a constant times $1+z$. On $[0,1]$ $\Psi_m$ is bounded.

<a id="warm:moment-dissipation"></a>
<a id="warm:moment-layer-profile"></a>
For a strictly positive density $z$, define the corresponding dissipation $\mathcal D_m(z)=\mathcal E(z,\Psi_m'(z))$. We claim that, for $\mathsf M_m(z)$ above a fixed threshold, $$T_n\mathcal D_m(z)
       \ge c_{m,\xi}\mathsf M_m(z)^{m+2/3-\xi}.
                                                               \label{warm:moment-dissipation}$$ Put $V=\mathsf M_m(z)$ and use levels $d_j=(V/2)(1.1)^j$. If $V$ is large, the part of $\mu[z(\log_+z)^m]$ below $V/2$ is at most $2^{-m}V^m$. Geometric summation as in Lemma <a href="#warm:entropy-profile" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="warm:entropy-profile">22</a> gives a level $d\ge V/2$ with $$B=\mu[z\mathbf 1_{\{d\le\log z\le1.1d\}}]
       \ge c_m(V/d)^{m+0.1}.$$ Indeed otherwise $(1.1)^m\sum_jd_j^mB_j\le C_m c_m V^m$ would be too small. The test $u=\mathcal U_d(z)$ from Lemma <a href="#warm:log-layer" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="warm:log-layer">21</a> therefore satisfies <a href="#warm:restricted-class" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="warm:restricted-class">[warm:restricted-class]</a>, and <a href="#warm:modified-profile" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="warm:modified-profile">[warm:modified-profile]</a> gives $$T_n\mathcal I(u)\ge c\,\mu[u]L^{5/3-\xi}
       \ge cB d^{5/3-\xi}.                               \label{warm:moment-layer-profile}$$

We check that the new dissipation controls this layer with its additional weight $d^{m-1}$. On an edge write $a\ge b>0$, $x=\log a$, $y=\log b$. Then $$\Psi_m'(a)-\Psi_m'(b)
       =\int_y^x(1+|t|)^{m-1}\,\mathrm dt.$$ If $x\ge0.4d$, the last integral is at least $c_m d^{m-1}(x-y)$. To verify this uniformly in $y$, use the top half of $[0,x]$ when $-x\le y\le x/2$, the entire interval when $y\ge x/2$, and the negative half nearest $y$ when $y<-x$; in each case a fixed fraction of the interval has $|t|$ at least a fixed fraction of $x$. The two Lipschitz bounds in the proof of Lemma <a href="#warm:log-layer" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="warm:log-layer">21</a> then apply. If $x<0.4d$, both endpoints are in the lower branch of $\mathcal U_d$. On $[b,a]$ its derivative is at most $2e^{-0.4d}$, while its logarithm has slope two in log coordinates. Since $d^{m-1}e^{-0.4d}\le C_m$, the same conclusion follows using $(1+|t|)^{m-1}\ge1$. Thus in both cases $$d^{m-1}\bigl(\mathcal U_d(a)-\mathcal U_d(b)\bigr)
       \bigl(\log\mathcal U_d(a)-\log\mathcal U_d(b)\bigr)
 \le C_m(a-b)\bigl(\Psi_m'(a)-\Psi_m'(b)\bigr).$$ Summation gives $\mathcal D_m(z)\ge c_m d^{m-1}\mathcal I(u)$. Combining this with <a href="#warm:moment-layer-profile" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="warm:moment-layer-profile">[warm:moment-layer-profile]</a> and the lower bound on $B$, and using $2/3-\xi>0.1$, gives $$T_n\mathcal D_m(z)
 \ge cB d^{m+2/3-\xi}
 \ge c_m V^{m+0.1}d^{2/3-\xi-0.1}
 \ge c_m' V^{m+2/3-\xi}.$$ This proves <a href="#warm:moment-dissipation" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="warm:moment-dissipation">[warm:moment-dissipation]</a>.

Along the finite semigroup at positive times, $$\frac{\,\mathrm d}{\,\mathrm ds}V_m(w_s^\rho)
       =-T_n\mathcal D_m(w_s^\rho).$$ Equations <a href="#warm:moment-comparison" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="warm:moment-comparison">[warm:moment-comparison]</a>–<a href="#warm:moment-dissipation" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="warm:moment-dissipation">[warm:moment-dissipation]</a> give, above a fixed threshold, $$\frac{\,\mathrm d}{\,\mathrm ds}V_m(w_s^\rho)
       \le-c V_m(w_s^\rho)^{1+(2/3-\xi)/m}.$$ Integrating from an earlier positive time and letting that time decrease to zero yields $V_m(w_s^\rho)\le C(1+s^{-m/(2/3-\xi)})$. The comparison <a href="#warm:moment-comparison" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="warm:moment-comparison">[warm:moment-comparison]</a> proves <a href="#warm:log-moment" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="warm:log-moment">[warm:log-moment]</a>. This argument allows initial zeros, because $\Psi_m$ is continuous at zero and the kernel is strictly positive afterward.

The three conclusions <a href="#warm:entropy" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="warm:entropy">[warm:entropy]</a>–<a href="#warm:log-moment" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="warm:log-moment">[warm:log-moment]</a> depend only on the off-diagonal couplings. Let $\mathcal G_n^{\rm aug}$ be the final event in the augmented Gaussian space, and put $$\mathcal G_n^{\rm off}
 =\left\{W_{\rm off}:
       \mathbb P(\mathcal G_n^{\rm aug}\mid W_{\rm off})>0\right\}.$$ Then $\mathbb P(\mathcal G_n^{\rm off})\ge
\mathbb P(\mathcal G_n^{\rm aug})$. For fixed off-diagonal couplings the three inequalities are deterministic, so their validity on an augmented realization in $\mathcal G_n^{\rm aug}$ descends to $\mathcal G_n^{\rm off}$. Taking this as the theorem event proves the stated disorder quantifiers. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-warm-kernel-log-tail"></a>
<div id="warm:kernel-log-tail" class="corollary">

<a id="warm:kernel-tail"></a>
**Corollary 24** (A polynomial tail bound for the heat-kernel logarithm). *Fix $\beta>0$, $A>0$, $0<C_\star<\infty$, and $\vartheta>0$. On Gaussian disorder events of limiting lower probability at least $1-\vartheta$, with a fixed constant $C$, $$\sup_{\sigma}\ \sup_{1\le d\le C_\star T_n}
 \sum_\tau P_d(\sigma,\tau)
 \mathbf 1_{\left\{\log p_d(\sigma,\tau)>
       \frac12 n^\beta(T_n/d)^{3/2}\right\}}
 \le Cn^{-A}                                                \label{warm:kernel-tail}$$ for all sufficiently large $n$. For any initial law $\rho$, averaging the displayed row probabilities over $\sigma\sim\rho$ preserves the same bound.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-warm-kernel-log-tail"><summary>Proof of stmt-warm-kernel-log-tail</summary>

*Proof.* Choose $\xi>0$ so small that $$\frac{\xi}{2/3-\xi}<\frac{\beta}{2},$$ then choose a fixed integer $m>2A/\beta$. Apply <a href="#warm:log-moment" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="warm:log-moment">[warm:log-moment]</a> to the point initial law at $\sigma$ and time $s=d/T_n$. Set $v=T_n/d$. Uniformly for $1\le d\le C_\star T_n$, so $C_\star^{-1}\le v\le n^{2/3}$, $$\frac{1+v^{1/(2/3-\xi)}}{n^\beta v^{3/2}}
 \le C_{\xi,C_\star}
       n^{-\beta+\xi/(2/3-\xi)}
 \le C_{\xi,C_\star}n^{-\beta/2}.$$ Markov’s inequality under the transition law $P_d(\sigma,\tau)=\mu(\tau)p_d(\sigma,\tau)$ now bounds the left side of <a href="#warm:kernel-tail" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="warm:kernel-tail">[warm:kernel-tail]</a> by $$\left(
 \frac{2\{1+\mu[p_d(\sigma,\cdot)
                  (\log_+p_d(\sigma,\cdot))^m]\}^{1/m}}
      {n^\beta(T_n/d)^{3/2}}\right)^m
 \le C_m n^{-m\beta/2}\le C_m n^{-A}.$$ The choices of $\xi,m$ are fixed in that order before $n$. The statement for $\sigma\sim\rho$ follows by averaging these row-specific probabilities. ◻

</details>

<a id="sec:gaussian-limits"></a>
### Positive-time Gaussian limits and the uniform start

Two inputs give the positive-time edge evolution. For bounded cylinder sources, the finite Markov resolvent contraction bounds the optimizers used in the stationary relaxed-energy theorem. A variational argument then gives the required strong semigroup convergence. The warming kernel bound controls the evolved densities, whose weak limits inherit that evolution. Warming also controls the total mass in a growing block of edge modes. A rotation argument distributes that mass among individual modes and retains information specific to the uniform start.

Throughout this section we use Gaussian couplings and the completed GOE matrix of Section <a href="#sec:background" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:background">2</a>, writing $\Lambda=\mathop{\mathrm{diag}}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n)$. Write $w_{n,s}=d(\nu_nP_{sT_n})/d\mu$ when the system size needs emphasis. We use the represented-subsequence convention of that section and denote the probability and expectation on a representation by $\widehat{\mathbb P}$ and $\widehat{\mathbb E}$.

<a id="stmt-prop-gaussian-subsequence"></a>
<div id="prop:gaussian-subsequence" class="proposition">

**Proposition 25** (Positive-time Gaussian subsequential limits). *Every sequence of Gaussian system sizes tending to infinity has a further represented subsequence on which the following assertions hold almost surely. The edge coordinates converge to $g$, and there is a measurable random family $h_s\in L^2(\Pi_g)$, $s>0$, with the following properties. The family may at this stage depend on the represented data in addition to $g$.*

<a id="glim:density-family"></a>
<a id="glim:limit-kernel"></a>
*There is a finite random $C\ge1$, independent of $s,t$, such that $$0\le h_s\le \mathcal K(s):=C\exp(C s^{-77/50}),\qquad
 \Pi_g[h_s]=1,\qquad
 h_{s+t}=S^g_t h_s,\qquad s,t>0,
 \label{glim:density-family}$$ where $S^g_t=\exp(-t c_*H_g)$. The map $s\mapsto h_s$ is continuous in $L^2(\Pi_g)$. For each $t>0$, $S^g_t$ has a nonnegative symmetric kernel $k_t^g$ relative to $\Pi_g$ satisfying $$0\le k_t^g(x,y)\le \mathcal K(t)
 \quad\text{for \(\Pi_g\otimes\Pi_g\)-almost every \((x,y)\)}.
 \label{glim:limit-kernel}$$ The constant $77/50$ is the exponent $1.54$ in Theorem <a href="#thm:warming" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:warming">15</a>.*

<a id="glim:functional-subsequence"></a>
<a id="glim:correlation-series"></a>
<a id="glim:relaxation"></a>
*On this subsequence, $$A_{n,J}\longrightarrow A_g
 \quad\text{in }C_{\mathrm{loc}}((0,\infty)),\qquad
 B_{n,J}\longrightarrow B_h
 \quad\text{in }C_{\mathrm{loc}}((0,\infty)^2),
 \label{glim:functional-subsequence}$$ where $$B_h(s,t)=\sum_{a\ge1}\Pi_g[h_s x_a\,S^g_t x_a].
 \label{glim:correlation-series}$$ The series in <a href="#glim:correlation-series" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="glim:correlation-series">[glim:correlation-series]</a> converges locally uniformly and is continuous. Finally, $$\|h_s-1\|_{L^2(\Pi_g)}\longrightarrow0,\qquad
 B_h(s,\cdot)\longrightarrow A_g(\cdot)
 \quad\text{in }C_{\mathrm{loc}}((0,\infty))
 \quad(s\to\infty).
 \label{glim:relaxation}$$*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-prop-gaussian-subsequence"><summary>Proof of stmt-prop-gaussian-subsequence</summary>

*Proof.* We first pass the semigroups on bounded sources, then construct the densities, and finally justify the sum over all edge coordinates.

<a id="pm-h-22"></a>
###### Varying $L^2$ spaces.

Choose a countable family $\mathcal{C}$ of smooth compact cylinders with this approximation property: every smooth compact cylinder is approximated uniformly, together with its first derivatives, by elements of $\mathcal{C}$ supported in one fixed compact coordinate set. Rational smooth approximations on rational boxes give such a family. The stated approximation and the definition of the closed form make $\mathcal{C}$ dense in its form norm, and also dense in $L^2(\Pi_g)$. For linear tests put $\mathcal{V}=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb Q}(\mathcal{C}\cup\{1\})$. This is a countable family of bounded smooth cylinders, dense in $L^1(\Pi_g)$ and $L^2(\Pi_g)$. If $\phi\in\mathcal{V}$ depends on the first $d$ coordinates, let $\phi_n=\phi(x_1,\ldots,x_d)$ on the finite cube.

<a id="glim:static-pairings"></a>
<a id="glim:common-approximation"></a>
The static cylinder and moment convergence of (OpenAI 2026d, Corollary 3.3) <a id="pm-cite-84"></a>[[FUA](#ref-FUA)] gives $$\mu[\phi_n\psi_n]\longrightarrow\Pi_g[\phi\psi]
 \quad(\phi,\psi\in\mathcal{V}).
 \label{glim:static-pairings}$$ On sequences bounded in $L^2(\mu)$, the weak convergence of Section <a href="#sec:background" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:background">2</a> can be tested on this countable family: the pairings with every $\phi\in\mathcal{V}$ converge to the corresponding pairings with $f$ if and only if the pairings with every smooth compact cylinder do. To pass from $\mathcal{V}$ to an arbitrary smooth compact cylinder, approximate it uniformly on a common support by $\mathcal{C}$, and use the uniform $L^2$ bound to control the pairing error in both spaces. The converse follows from the same approximation, with cutoffs tending to one for the constant test. A sequence bounded in $L^2(\mu)$ has a weakly convergent subsequence: diagonal extraction of its pairings defines a bounded linear functional on the cylinder span by <a href="#glim:static-pairings" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="glim:static-pairings">[glim:static-pairings]</a>, and the Riesz representation theorem supplies its $L^2(\Pi_g)$ representative. The same argument gives $$\|f\|_{L^2(\Pi_g)}\le\liminf_n\|f_n\|_{L^2(\mu)}.$$ As in Section <a href="#sec:background" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:background">2</a>, the convergence is strong when the norms also converge. For such a sequence, $$\lim_n\|f_n-\phi_n\|_{L^2(\mu)}^2
       =\|f-\phi\|_{L^2(\Pi_g)}^2
       \quad(\phi\in\mathcal{C}).
 \label{glim:common-approximation}$$ Consequently strong convergence is equivalent to approximation, in both spaces, by the same cylinders. In particular, the pairing of an $L^2$-bounded weakly convergent sequence with a strongly convergent sequence converges.

<a id="pm-h-23"></a>
###### Resolvents from bounded optimizers.

<a id="glim:optimizer-liminf"></a>
Set $$\mathfrak q_n=T_n\mathcal E,\quad \mathfrak A_n=T_nH_n,\qquad
 \mathfrak q=c_*\Pi_g[|\nabla\cdot|^2],\quad \mathfrak A=c_*H_g.$$ For $\phi\in\mathcal{C}$ and rational $z>0$, consider $$u_n=(z+\mathfrak A_n)^{-1}\phi_n,\qquad
 u=(z+\mathfrak A)^{-1}\phi.$$ The finite Markov property gives $\|u_n\|_\infty\le z^{-1}\|\phi\|_\infty$. The resolvent identity also bounds $\|u_n\|_2$ and $\mathfrak q_n(u_n)$ uniformly. Thus these particular optimizers satisfy the polynomial supremum bound as well as the norm and energy bounds in the relaxed-energy theorem (OpenAI 2026d, Theorem 6.8) <a id="pm-cite-85"></a>[[FUA](#ref-FUA)]. That theorem applies to disorder-dependent tests under the class-uniform quenched convention recorded in Section <a href="#sec:background" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:background">2</a>. This proof invokes it only for the countably specified optimizer sequences, one for each $\phi\in\mathcal{C}$ and rational $z>0$, on their common represented event. Its lower bound therefore gives $$\liminf_n\mathfrak q_n(u_n)\ge\mathfrak q(U)
 \quad\text{whenever \(u_n\) has weak limit \(U\)}.
 \label{glim:optimizer-liminf}$$

Here is the variational passage, including the norm conclusion. Let $$v_n=\sup_f\{2\langle\phi_n,f\rangle_\mu-z\|f\|_2^2-\mathfrak q_n(f)\}
     =\langle\phi_n,u_n\rangle_\mu
     =z\|u_n\|_2^2+\mathfrak q_n(u_n),$$ and define $v$ by the analogous supremum in $L^2(\Pi_g)$. Take an optimizer subsequence attaining the upper limit and then a weak limit $U$. The norm lower bound and <a href="#glim:optimizer-liminf" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="glim:optimizer-liminf">[glim:optimizer-liminf]</a> imply $$\limsup_n v_n
 \le 2\langle\phi,U\rangle_{\Pi_g}
       -z\|U\|_2^2-\mathfrak q(U)
 \le v.$$ For the reverse inequality, take $F\in\mathcal{C}$. The recovery part of (OpenAI 2026d, Theorem 6.8) <a id="pm-cite-86"></a>[[FUA](#ref-FUA)] supplies, for each fixed recovery index $j$, polynomially bounded finite functions strongly converging to $F$, whose energies converge to $\mathfrak q(F)$ in the order $n\to\infty$, then $j\to\infty$. Testing the variational supremum with these functions in exactly that order gives $$\liminf_n v_n\ge
 2\langle\phi,F\rangle_{\Pi_g}-z\|F\|_2^2-\mathfrak q(F).$$ The form density of $\mathcal{C}$ allows the supremum over $F$, proving $v_n\to v$. Only the countably many sources in $\mathcal{C}$ and rational $z$ are used on the common source event. The limiting variational problem is strictly concave, so every weak optimizer limit is its unique optimizer $u$. Moreover, $$\limsup_n z\|u_n\|_2^2
 \le v-\mathfrak q(u)=z\|u\|_2^2.$$ Together with norm lower semicontinuity this proves strong convergence of $u_n$ to $u$. This is the bounded-source version of the variational argument in (OpenAI 2026d, proof of Lemma 7.2) <a id="pm-cite-87"></a>[[FUA](#ref-FUA)].

<a id="glim:semigroup-strong"></a>
The bound $\|(z+\mathfrak A_n)^{-1}\|_{2\to2}\le z^{-1}$ and <a href="#glim:common-approximation" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="glim:common-approximation">[glim:common-approximation]</a> now extend this resolvent convergence to every strongly converging input. No additional use of the lower energy bound is needed for that extension. To pass to semigroups, put $R_n=(1+\mathfrak A_n)^{-1}$, $R=(1+\mathfrak A)^{-1}$, and, for $t>0$, define on $[0,1]$ $$F_t(q)=
 \begin{cases}
 \exp[-t(q^{-1}-1)],&q>0,\\
 0,&q=0.
 \end{cases}$$ This function is continuous. Polynomial approximation of $F_t$ and convergence of every power of $R_n$ on strongly converging inputs prove $$P_{t_nT_n}f_n\longrightarrow S^g_t f
 \quad\text{strongly whenever \(f_n\to f\) strongly and \(t_n\to t>0\)}.
 \label{glim:semigroup-strong}$$ For the assertion with varying times, use $$\sup_{\lambda\ge0}|e^{-t\lambda}-e^{-u\lambda}|
 \le\frac{|t-u|}{e\delta},\qquad t,u\ge\delta>0.$$ This proof identifies the limit of $P_{tT_n}$ as $\exp(-t c_*H_g)$ with the stated $T_n=n^{2/3}$.

<a id="pm-h-24"></a>
###### Densities and the limiting kernel.

<a id="glim:finite-density"></a>
On the represented sequence, Theorem <a href="#thm:warming" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:warming">15</a>, with fixed admissible auxiliary parameters, gives a finite random $C$ and numbers $\delta_n\downarrow0$ such that $\|P_{sT_n}\|_{1\to\infty}\le \mathcal K(s)$ for all $s\ge\delta_n$. Since $w_{n,0}$ is a nonnegative density and the semigroup is self-adjoint, $$0\le w_{n,s}\le \mathcal K(s),\qquad
 \mu[w_{n,s}]=1,\qquad \|w_{n,s}\|_2^2\le \mathcal K(s)
 \quad(s\ge\delta_n).
 \label{glim:finite-density}$$ Include the pairings of these densities with $\mathcal{V}$ at each positive rational $s$ in the representation. Every limit functional $L_s$ obeys $$|L_s(\phi)|\le \mathcal K(s)\Pi_g[|\phi|],\qquad
 L_s(\phi)\ge-\mathcal K(s)\Pi_g[\phi^-],\qquad L_s(1)=1.$$ Here $\phi^-=\max\{-\phi,0\}$.
