The bound follows from <a href="#glim:finite-density" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="glim:finite-density">[glim:finite-density]</a> and static convergence also for the continuous cylinders $|\phi|$ and $\phi^-$. It extends $L_s$ to $L^1(\Pi_g)$. The second inequality proves positivity of the extension: if cylinders $\phi_j$ converge in $L^1$ to $f\ge0$, then $\Pi_g[\phi_j^-]\le\|\phi_j-f\|_1\to0$. The extension is therefore represented by a density $0\le h_s\le \mathcal K(s)$ of mass one. In particular $\|h_s\|_2^2\le \mathcal K(s)$. This also justifies normalization if only compact cylinders were initially retained: their cutoffs tending to one have complements bounded by $\mathcal K(s)$ times the corresponding static probabilities. Measurability can be seen concretely. Take nested finite cylinder partitions which generate the product Borel sets and whose cell boundaries have zero $\Pi_g$ measure; rational coordinate boxes have this property by the cylinder densities of (OpenAI 2026d, Proposition 2.3) <a id="pm-cite-88"></a>[[FUA](#ref-FUA)]. The value $L_s(\mathbf 1_A)$ for each cell is a measurable limit of its values on fixed smooth approximations to $\mathbf 1_A$, which can in turn be approximated by $\mathcal{C}$. On each cell $A$ put the ratio $L_s(\mathbf 1_A)/\Pi_g(A)$, with value zero if the denominator is zero. These ratios are measurable, bounded by $\mathcal K(s)$, and are the conditional expectations of $h_s$ on the nested partitions. Their bounded martingale limit gives a measurable representative of $h_s$.

For positive rational $s,t$, reversibility and <a href="#glim:semigroup-strong" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="glim:semigroup-strong">[glim:semigroup-strong]</a> imply for every $\phi\in\mathcal{C}$ $$\Pi_g[h_{s+t}\phi]
 =\lim_n\mu[w_{n,s}P_{tT_n}\phi_n]
 =\Pi_g[h_sS^g_t\phi].$$ We used the weak–strong pairing rule; the $w_{n,s}$ are weakly convergent and bounded in $L^2$. Hence $h_{s+t}=S^g_t h_s$. The closed cylinder-gradient form is a Dirichlet form: smooth normal contractions obey its contraction inequality, and closure preserves it. Constants belong to the form and have zero energy, by (OpenAI 2026d, Proposition 5.1) <a id="pm-cite-89"></a>[[FUA](#ref-FUA)]. Thus $S^g_t$ is Markov and preserves one. For a real $s>0$, choose a rational $q<s$ and set $h_s=S^g_{s-q}h_q$. The rational relation makes this definition independent of $q$. Strong continuity of the semigroup proves $L^2$ continuity in $s>0$, as well as the relation for all $s,t>0$. Positivity and mass one persist. Taking rationals $q\uparrow s$ in the density bound, using $L^2$ convergence and an almost-everywhere subsequence, proves $h_s\le \mathcal K(s)$. For deterministic dyadic rationals $q_j(s)\to s$, every cylinder integral at $s$ is the limit of its measurable values at $q_j(s)$. It is therefore jointly measurable in the environment and $s$. The same partition construction therefore gives jointly measurable representatives for the real-time family.

<a id="glim:time-equicontinuity"></a>
The finite convergence against cylinders also holds along every sequence $s_n\to s>0$. Indeed, for $s\ge\delta>0$, the identity $w_{n,s}=P_{(s-\delta/2)T_n}w_{n,\delta/2}$ and spectral calculus give $$\|\partial_s w_{n,s}\|_2
 \le \frac{2}{e\delta}\sqrt{\mathcal K(\delta/2)}
 \quad(n\ \text{sufficiently large}).
 \label{glim:time-equicontinuity}$$ Approximation of $s$ by a rational time, followed by the weak convergence there and the $L^2$ continuity of $h_s$, proves the claim.

For completeness we obtain the kernel needed to sum coordinates. For nonnegative smooth compact cylinders $\phi,\psi$, the finite kernel bound yields $$0\le\mu[\phi_nP_{tT_n}\psi_n]
       \le \mathcal K(t)\mu[\phi_n]\mu[\psi_n].$$ Passing to the limit using <a href="#glim:semigroup-strong" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="glim:semigroup-strong">[glim:semigroup-strong]</a>, and then approximating indicators in $L^2(\Pi_g)$, gives the same inequality with $\Pi_g[\phi S^g_t\psi]$ in place of the left side. Define on rectangles the nonnegative functional $$\mathbf 1_{A\times B}\longmapsto
       \Pi_g[\mathbf 1_AS^g_t\mathbf 1_B].$$ For a simple function on rectangles use common disjoint partitions of the two factors. The preceding rectangle inequality then bounds the functional on every nonnegative such function by $\mathcal K(t)$ times its $L^1(\Pi_g\otimes\Pi_g)$ norm. It extends to a positive bounded functional on that $L^1$ space, so has a density $k_t^g$ with $0\le k_t^g\le \mathcal K(t)$. Self-adjointness makes the density symmetric. Its marginals are $\Pi_g$, since $S^g_t1=1$. This proves <a href="#glim:limit-kernel" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="glim:limit-kernel">[glim:limit-kernel]</a>; it does not require a joint pointwise version of the kernels for all $t$.

<a id="pm-h-25"></a>
###### The tail of two equilibrium copies.

<a id="glim:static-tail"></a>
Let $x_a'=x_a(\sigma')$, and set $$Q_{n,m}(\sigma,\sigma')=\sum_{a>m}x_a x_a',\qquad
 V_{n,m}=(\mu\otimes\mu)[Q_{n,m}^2].$$ To see why this equilibrium quantity controls the quench trace, define the relative transition kernel and the two-time density $$p_{n,t}(\sigma,\sigma')
   =\frac{P_{tT_n}(\sigma,\sigma')}{\mu(\sigma')},\qquad
 d_{n,s,t}(\sigma,\sigma')
   =w_{n,s}(\sigma)p_{n,t}(\sigma,\sigma').$$ The latter is the density of the two spins at times $sT_n$ and $(s+t)T_n$ relative to $\mu\otimes\mu$. On every compact subset of $s,t>0$, the warming bounds give a uniform bound on this density for all sufficiently large $n$ on the represented sequence. Hence $$\left|\sum_{a>m}\mu[w_{n,s}x_aP_{tT_n}x_a]\right|
 =\left|(\mu\otimes\mu)[d_{n,s,t}Q_{n,m}]\right|
 \le\|d_{n,s,t}\|_{L^2(\mu\otimes\mu)}V_{n,m}^{1/2}.$$ The stationary trace has the same bound with $d_{n,s,t}$ replaced by $p_{n,t}$. Thus it suffices to control $V_{n,m}$ uniformly as $m$ increases. We claim that the representation may be further extracted so that $$\lim_{m\to\infty}\limsup_n V_{n,m}=0
 \quad\text{almost surely}.
 \label{glim:static-tail}$$ Recall $r_n=n^{-1/3+10^{-4}}$ from Section <a href="#sec:edge-estimates" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:edge-estimates">3</a>, and fix the spectrum in one of the tight spectral sets of (OpenAI 2026d, Proposition 2.3) <a id="pm-cite-90"></a>[[FUA](#ref-FUA)]. In this paragraph take its canonical parameters $$b_n^\circ=1+(-g_{1,n})_+,\qquad
 b^\circ=1+(-g_1)_+,\qquad
 \ell_{a,n}^\circ=(g_{a,n}+b_n^\circ)^{-1}.$$ Let $\mu^{\mathrm{sp}}$ be the spherical Gibbs law, and $L_\circ=Z_{\mathrm{cube}}/Z_{\mathrm{sp}}$, with both partition functions relative to their normalized uniform measures. Average over the full Haar eigenframe at this fixed spectrum. Multiplication by $L_\circ^2$ cancels the two cube Gibbs denominators. In the uncapped replica comparison of (OpenAI 2026d, Lemma 3.2) <a id="pm-cite-91"></a>[[FUA](#ref-FUA)], the normalized contribution of pairs with $|\rho|=|n^{-1}\sigma\cdot\sigma'|>C r_n$ is at most $C e^{-c n r_n^3}$. Since $|Q_{n,m}|^2\le n^{2/3}$, inserting this square in the discarded part costs at most $C n^{2/3}e^{-c n r_n^3}$.

On the retained overlaps, the same comparison can be used with this square inserted. Here are the required uniform details. Conditional on $\rho$, a Haar-rotated cube pair and a spherical pair have the same law of an orthonormal sum-and-difference frame $(q,q')$. Their spectral vectors can be written $$Y(\rho)=\sqrt{\frac n2}
       \big(\sqrt{1+\rho}\,q+\sqrt{1-\rho}\,q'\big),\qquad
 Y'(\rho)=\sqrt{\frac n2}
       \big(\sqrt{1+\rho}\,q-\sqrt{1-\rho}\,q'\big).$$ The ratio of the discrete overlap mass and the spherical mass on a cell of width $2/n$ is at most $\exp(C+C n\rho^4)$, by the replica comparison. This is bounded on $|\rho|\le C r_n$, because $n r_n^4=o(1)$. The tilt exponent on this frame is $$\frac n2\big((1+\rho)q^{\mathsf T}\Lambda q
                    +(1-\rho){q'}^{\mathsf T}\Lambda q'\big).$$ Its oscillation in a cell is bounded when $\|\Lambda\|$ is bounded. If $\rho,\widetilde\rho$ lie in that cell, the displayed vectors change in Euclidean norm by at most $C n^{-1/2}$. After multiplying by $n^{-1/3}$, each vector changes by at most $C n^{-5/6}$ and has norm $n^{1/6}$. Projection onto the coordinates $a>m$ therefore gives, uniformly in $m$, $$|Q_{n,m}(\rho)-Q_{n,m}(\widetilde\rho)|\le C n^{-2/3}.$$ The inequality $(u+v)^2\le2u^2+2v^2$ now bounds the inserted square by the corresponding spherical square and $C n^{-4/3}$, up to the preceding bounded comparison factors.

<a id="glim:tail-probability"></a>
Under two independent spherical Gibbs laws, sign symmetry kills the cross terms in that square. The uniform coordinate moment bound in (OpenAI 2026d, Proposition 2.3) <a id="pm-cite-92"></a>[[FUA](#ref-FUA)] gives $$(\mu^{\mathrm{sp}}\otimes\mu^{\mathrm{sp}})[Q_{n,m}^2]
 =\sum_{a>m}\big(\mu^{\mathrm{sp}}[x_a^2]\big)^2
 \le C\sum_{a>m}(\ell_{a,n}^\circ)^2.$$ Since $\mathbf 1_{\{L_\circ\ge1/2\}}\le4L_\circ^2$, the comparison just proved yields <a id="glim:tail-haar"></a>$$\mathbb E_U[\mathbf 1_{\{L_\circ\ge1/2\}}V_{n,m}]
 \le C\sum_{a>m}(\ell_{a,n}^\circ)^2
       +C n^{-4/3}+C n^{2/3}e^{-c n r_n^3}.
 \label{glim:tail-haar}$$ The constants are uniform on the retained spectral set. The squared resolvent tails tend to zero as $m\to\infty$ there, and $n r_n^3$ is a positive power of $n$. Also $\mathbb P_U\{L_\circ<1/2\}=o(1)$, by (OpenAI 2026d, Lemma 2.5) <a id="pm-cite-93"></a>[[FUA](#ref-FUA)]. Markov’s inequality, followed by exhaustion of the tight spectral sets, proves for every $\epsilon>0$ $$\lim_{m\to\infty}\limsup_n
       \mathbb P\{V_{n,m}>\epsilon\}=0.
 \label{glim:tail-probability}$$ The same estimates make $V_{n,m}$ tight for every fixed $m$. Include these countably many quantities in the representation and extract coordinatewise limits $V_m$. The identity $$V_{n,m}=\sum_{a,b>m}\mu[x_ax_b]^2$$ shows that $V_{n,m}$, and hence $V_m$, decreases with $m$. Equation <a href="#glim:tail-probability" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="glim:tail-probability">[glim:tail-probability]</a> forces $V_m\downarrow0$ almost surely. Since $V_{n,m}\to V_m$ for each fixed $m$, this is <a href="#glim:static-tail" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="glim:static-tail">[glim:static-tail]</a>.

<a id="glim:limit-static-tail"></a>
The limiting version follows directly from the same sign symmetry and moments. With $\ell_a^\circ=(g_a+b^\circ)^{-1}$, for $M>m$, $$\left\|\sum_{m<a\le M}x_a x_a'\right\|_{L^2(\Pi_g\otimes\Pi_g)}^2
 =\sum_{m<a\le M}\Pi_g[x_a^2]^2
 \le C\sum_{a>m}(\ell_a^\circ)^2\longrightarrow0.
 \label{glim:limit-static-tail}$$ Thus these interval sums have an $L^2(\Pi_g\otimes\Pi_g)$ tail whose norm tends to zero.

<a id="pm-h-26"></a>
###### Correlation limits and relaxation.

Orthogonality of the eigenframe gives the exact finite identities $$A_{n,J}(t)=\sum_{a=1}^n\mu[x_aP_{tT_n}x_a],\qquad
 B_{n,J}(s,t)=\sum_{a=1}^n\mu[w_{n,s}x_aP_{tT_n}x_a].$$ The preceding two-copy reduction and <a href="#glim:static-tail" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="glim:static-tail">[glim:static-tail]</a> give uniform finite correlation tails on every compact positive time set. For the limiting series, the corresponding two-time density is $h_s(x)k_t^g(x,x')$ relative to $\Pi_g\otimes\Pi_g$; for the stationary series it is $k_t^g(x,x')$. Equations <a href="#glim:density-family" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="glim:density-family">[glim:density-family]</a> and <a href="#glim:limit-kernel" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="glim:limit-kernel">[glim:limit-kernel]</a> bound these densities uniformly on compact positive time sets. The same Cauchy–Schwarz argument with <a href="#glim:limit-static-tail" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="glim:limit-static-tail">[glim:limit-static-tail]</a> therefore gives the limiting uniform tail control.

It remains to pass each fixed summand. Static convergence of the mixed pairings $x_a\phi$ and the second moment $x_a^2$ makes the finite coordinate $x_a$ strongly convergent to the limiting $x_a$. If $s_n\to s>0$, then $w_{n,s_n}x_a$ is weakly convergent to $h_sx_a$. To see this, test first against a cylinder times a smooth cutoff of $x_a$ at height $R$, and use the convergence after <a href="#glim:time-equicontinuity" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="glim:time-equicontinuity">[glim:time-equicontinuity]</a>, extended from $\mathcal{C}$ by the common-support approximation above. For a bounded cylinder $\phi$, the omitted part of the pairing is at most $$\mathcal K(\delta)\|\phi\|_\infty
       \mu[|x_a|\mathbf 1_{\{|x_a|>R\}}]
 \le \frac{\mathcal K(\delta)\|\phi\|_\infty}{R}\mu[x_a^2]
 \quad(s_n\ge\delta).$$ The fixed second moments are bounded and converge, so this error vanishes uniformly as $R\to\infty$. Also $\|w_{n,s_n}x_a\|_2\le \mathcal K(\delta)\|x_a\|_2$. The weak–strong pairing rule and <a href="#glim:semigroup-strong" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="glim:semigroup-strong">[glim:semigroup-strong]</a> now give, whenever $s_n\to s>0$ and $t_n\to t>0$, $$\mu[w_{n,s_n}x_aP_{t_nT_n}x_a]
       \longrightarrow \Pi_g[h_sx_aS^g_t x_a].$$ The same argument without $w_{n,s_n}$ gives the fixed stationary summand. Each limiting summand is continuous. For $t\ge\delta>0$, the kernel bound gives $$\|S^g_t x_a\|_\infty\le \mathcal K(\delta)\Pi_g[|x_a|],\qquad
 \|x_aS^g_t x_a\|_2\le \mathcal K(\delta)\|x_a\|_2^2.$$ Thus $L^2$ continuity of $h_s$ gives continuity in $s$, uniformly for $t$ in positive compact intervals. Strong continuity of $S^g_t x_a$, paired with $h_sx_a\in L^2(\Pi_g)$, gives continuity in $t$. The uniform tail bound proves the asserted continuity and local uniform convergence of the full series. It also proves the two locally uniform finite limits in <a href="#glim:functional-subsequence" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="glim:functional-subsequence">[glim:functional-subsequence]</a>: failure of uniform convergence on a compact set would provide a sequence of time points with a convergent subsequence, contradicting the fixed-summand convergence, the uniform tails, and continuity of the limiting sum.

Finally, the kernel of $H_g$ consists exactly of the constants, by (OpenAI 2026d, Proposition 5.1) <a id="pm-cite-94"></a>[[FUA](#ref-FUA)]. The spectral theorem and $h_s=S^g_{s-s_0}h_{s_0}$ give $h_s\to\Pi_g[h_{s_0}]=1$ in $L^2(\Pi_g)$. For each fixed $a$, the last displayed bound implies, uniformly for $t\ge\delta$, $$|\Pi_g[(h_s-1)x_aS^g_t x_a]|
 \le \mathcal K(\delta)\|x_a\|_2^2\|h_s-1\|_2\longrightarrow0.$$ The correlation tails are uniform also for $s\ge s_0$, since $\|h_s\|_\infty\le \mathcal K(s_0)$. Passing first through a finite sum and then letting its length tend to infinity proves <a href="#glim:relaxation" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="glim:relaxation">[glim:relaxation]</a>. ◻

</details>

The preceding proposition does not yet identify the family as a function of $g$. The following estimate retains the information from the finite uniform initialization that will make this identification possible.

<a id="stmt-prop-uniform-seed-escape"></a>
<div id="prop:uniform-seed-escape" class="proposition">

<a id="glim:rates"></a>
<a id="glim:weighted-size"></a>
**Proposition 26** (An escape estimate from the uniform start). *There is a measurable admissible choice $b=b(g)$ such that, almost surely, $$r_a:=g_a+b>0,\qquad D_g(b)>0,\qquad
 c_g(1+a)^{2/3}\le r_a\le C_g(1+a)^{2/3}\quad(a\ge1)
 \label{glim:rates}$$ for finite positive $c_g,C_g$. Define $$M_g(x)=\frac12\sum_{a\ge1}\frac{x_a^2}{r_a}.
 \label{glim:weighted-size}$$ Then $0<M_g<\infty$ $\Pi_g$-almost surely. Choose a Borel full-measure set of edge realizations on which these assertions about $b$, $r_a$, and $M_g$ hold, with $b$ Borel there and $r_a=g_a+b$. On the product of this edge set with $\mathbb R^\mathbb N$, $M_g$ is an extended nonnegative Borel function of $(g,x)$, since its jointly Borel partial sums increase to it. In every escape event, $x_i^2/M_g(x)$ denotes the quotient on the subset where $0<M_g(x)<\infty$, extended by zero to all remaining pairs in $\mathbb R^\mathbb N\times\mathbb R^\mathbb N$. This version is jointly Borel and agrees with the usual quotient $\Pi_g$-almost surely for every $g$ in the chosen edge set.*

<a id="glim:seed-escape"></a>
*For every represented family in Proposition <a href="#prop:gaussian-subsequence" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:gaussian-subsequence">25</a>, every fixed $i\ge1$, and every $\epsilon>0$, $$\lim_{s\downarrow0}
 \widehat{\mathbb E}\!\left[
    \Pi_g\!\left[h_s\mathbf 1_{\{x_i^2/M_g>\epsilon\}}\right]\right]=0.
 \label{glim:seed-escape}$$ Here the probability averages the represented environment as well as the draw from $h_s\Pi_g$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-prop-uniform-seed-escape"><summary>Proof of stmt-prop-uniform-seed-escape</summary>

*Proof.* We will show that $x_i^2>s^{13/20}$ has vanishing averaged probability under the limiting time-$s$ law, while $M_g<s^{14/25}$ also has vanishing averaged probability as $s\downarrow0$. Away from these two events, $x_i^2/M_g$ is at most $s^{9/100}$. We obtain the numerator bound from the finite uniform-start dynamics, then bound the denominator directly under the conditioned edge measure.

<a id="pm-h-27"></a>
###### The total mass in a block of finite modes.

Fix $\varepsilon>0$, and fix the auxiliary log-moment parameters in Theorem <a href="#thm:warming" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:warming">15</a> once and for all. Its entropy bound and Proposition <a href="#prop:edge-estimates" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:edge-estimates">3</a> provide a quenched disorder event $\mathcal G_{n,\varepsilon}$ of limiting probability at least $1-\varepsilon$ on which their constants and thresholds are fixed, the entropy bound holds simultaneously for every positive time, and the uncapped cube projection tails hold at every allowed scale. Separately retain a spectrum-only event $\mathcal S_{n,\varepsilon}$ of limiting probability at least $1-\varepsilon$ for the band estimates in Lemma <a href="#edge:spectral" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="edge:spectral">4</a> and the tight leading-edge bound $|g_{1,n}|\le C_\varepsilon$. The latter follows from the GOE edge convergence in Section <a href="#sec:background" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:background">2</a>. The constants in the following calculations may depend on $\varepsilon$.

<a id="glim:finite-head-spectrum"></a>
For $0<s<1$, put $m=\lceil s^{-5/4}\rceil$. For $n\ge m$, set <a id="glim:rotation-scales"></a>$$D_m(v)=\sum_{a\le m}x_a(v)^2,\qquad
 I=s^{47/100},\qquad R=s^{-53/100}.
 \label{glim:rotation-scales}$$ Here $x_a(v)$ is evaluated along the finite dynamics at physical time $vT_n$, and $I=sR$. Choose $k_p=np^3=C' m$, with the fixed $C'$ sufficiently large. Take $s$ small enough that $C'm$ exceeds the fixed threshold, and then take $n$ sufficiently large that $m\le n$ and $p\le r_n$. The spectral band estimates imply that $\dim\mathcal H_p\ge m$ on $\mathcal S_{n,\varepsilon}$, so $P_p$ contains the first $m$ coordinates and $g_{m,n}\le T_np^2=(C'm)^{2/3}$. Together with $|g_{1,n}|\le C_\varepsilon$, this gives on that event $$\max_{a\le m}|g_{a,n}|\le C m^{2/3}.
 \label{glim:finite-head-spectrum}$$ At a fixed $s$, the value of $k_p$ is fixed as $n\to\infty$; this is why the extension to the lowest scales in Proposition <a href="#prop:edge-estimates" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:edge-estimates">3</a> is used here.

<a id="glim:head-mass"></a>
On $\mathcal G_{n,\varepsilon}\cap\mathcal S_{n,\varepsilon}$ put $Y_p=\|P_p\sigma\|^2/M_p^2$. Its projection tail is $\mu\{Y_p>u\}\le C\exp(-a k_pu^3)$ for every $u\ge u_0$, with fixed $u_0$. Integration of this tail gives $$\log\mu\exp\!\left(\tfrac a2 k_pY_p^3\right)\le C k_p.$$ The entropy inequality for any probability density $w$ relative to $\mu$, followed by Hölder’s inequality, therefore gives $$\mu[wY_p]\le
 C\left(1+\big(\mathop{\mathrm{Ent}}_\mu(w)/k_p\big)^{1/3}\right).$$ Since $D_m\le n^{-2/3}M_p^2Y_p=k_p^{1/3}Y_p$, the entropy part of Theorem <a href="#thm:warming" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:warming">15</a> yields under the direct dynamical law at fixed disorder $$\mathbb E_{\nu_n}^J[D_m(v)]
 \le C\big(m^{1/3}+v^{-77/150}\big),\qquad 0<v\le s\le1.
 \label{glim:head-mass}$$ This use of entropy is entirely relative to the ordinary Gibbs law $\mu$; the path in this expectation starts from $\nu_n$.

<a id="glim:cutoff-loss"></a>
Let $Q(v)=\int_0^vD_m(w)\,dw$ and define the event $$G=\{Q(s)<I,\ D_m(s)\le R\}.$$ Integrating <a href="#glim:head-mass" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="glim:head-mass">[glim:head-mass]</a> and applying Markov’s inequality at the integral and the endpoint gives, on $\mathcal G_{n,\varepsilon}\cap\mathcal S_{n,\varepsilon}$, $$\mathbb P_{\nu_n}^J(G^c)
 \le C\big(s^{17/150}+s^{1/60}\big).
 \label{glim:cutoff-loss}$$ Indeed $m^{1/3}\le C s^{-5/12}$, and both comparisons use the same two positive powers: $$1-\frac5{12}-\frac{47}{100}
   =\frac{53}{100}-\frac5{12}=\frac{17}{150},\qquad
 1-\frac{77}{150}-\frac{47}{100}
   =\frac{53}{100}-\frac{77}{150}=\frac1{60}.$$

<a id="pm-h-28"></a>
###### A stopped rotation at fixed spectrum.

For this step fix only a spectrum satisfying <a href="#glim:finite-head-spectrum" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="glim:finite-head-spectrum">[glim:finite-head-spectrum]</a>. Let $\mathbb E_\Lambda$ average over the full conditional Haar law of $U$ and over the uniform-start heat-bath path. In particular, this expectation does not condition on $\mathcal G_{n,\varepsilon}$.

<a id="glim:path-likelihood"></a>
It is useful to specify the path likelihood. In normalized time $v$, take independent site clocks of rate $T_n$, a uniform initial spin, and an independent fair mark $\eta\in\{-1,1\}$ at every ring, including rings at which the mark equals the old spin. This is a reference law; the marked path is then determined without $U$. If the ring is at site $k$, its heat-bath probability is $$p_{U,k}(\eta\mid\sigma)=
 \frac{e^{\eta b_k(\sigma)}}{2\cosh b_k(\sigma)},\qquad
 b_k(\sigma)=\sum_{\ell\ne k}W_{k\ell}\sigma_\ell.$$ The likelihood of the dynamical path through $s$ relative to the reference law is $$\mathcal L_U=
 \prod_{\ell:v_\ell\le s}
 2p_{U,k_\ell}\big(\eta_\ell\mid\sigma(v_\ell-)\big).
 \label{glim:path-likelihood}$$ There is no initial or clock factor depending on $U$. This likelihood fixes the marked spin outcomes while the matrix varies; it permits differentiating the smooth heat-bath probabilities. The absence of an initial score is the feature of the uniform start used in this rotation.

<a id="glim:field-rotation"></a>
For $i,j\le m$, $i\ne j$, right-rotate these two columns with $\dot u_i=u_j$ and $\dot u_j=-u_i$. Then $$\dot x_i=x_j,\qquad \dot x_j=-x_i,\qquad
 \dot W=(\lambda_i-\lambda_j)
          (u_i u_j^{\mathsf T}+u_j u_i^{\mathsf T}).$$ Writing $\Delta_{ij}=\lambda_i-\lambda_j$, diagonal deletion in the physical local field gives $$\dot b_k=\Delta_{ij}\left[
  n^{1/3}(u_{j,k}x_i+u_{i,k}x_j)
                    -2u_{i,k}u_{j,k}\sigma_k\right].$$ Orthogonality and $\sum_k u_{i,k}^2u_{j,k}^2\le1$, together with $|\Delta_{ij}|=T_n^{-1}|g_{i,n}-g_{j,n}|
\le C n^{-2/3}m^{2/3}$, imply $$\sum_k\dot b_k^2
 \le C n^{-4/3}m^{4/3}
       \big[n^{2/3}(x_i^2+x_j^2)+1\big].
 \label{glim:field-rotation}$$ The final $1$ is the contribution from deleting the diagonal.

<a id="glim:rotation-score"></a>
In the filtration revealing $U$ initially and then the marked rings, the logarithmic derivative of $\mathcal L_U$ through $v$ is $$S_{ij}(v)=\sum_{\ell:v_\ell\le v}
  \big(\eta_\ell-\tanh b_{k_\ell}(\sigma(v_\ell-))\big)
                 \dot b_{k_\ell}(\sigma(v_\ell-)).$$ Under the dynamical law it is a square-integrable martingale. In fact each marked increment has conditional mean zero and conditional variance $\operatorname{sech}^2(b_k)\dot b_k^2$; its predictable bracket is $$\langle S_{ij}\rangle_v
 =T_n\int_0^v\sum_k\operatorname{sech}^2(b_k(\sigma(w-)))
                         \dot b_k(\sigma(w-))^2\,dw.$$ Define $$\tau=s\wedge\inf\{v:Q(v)\ge I\},\qquad
 I_a=\mathbb E_\Lambda\int_0^\tau x_a(v)^2\,dv\quad(a\le m).$$ The function $Q$ is continuous, so $Q(\tau)\le I$. Stopped martingale isometry and <a href="#glim:field-rotation" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="glim:field-rotation">[glim:field-rotation]</a> give $$\mathbb E_\Lambda[S_{ij}(\tau)^2]
 \le C m^{4/3}\big(I_i+I_j+s n^{-2/3}\big).
 \label{glim:rotation-score}$$

<a id="glim:haar-identity"></a>
For a fixed marked reference history, $D_m,Q,\tau$, and $G$ are exactly invariant under this rotation. Apply Haar invariance first to $$F_{ij}=\int_0^\tau x_i(v)x_j(v)\,dv.$$ Differentiating its integral with likelihood <a href="#glim:path-likelihood" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="glim:path-likelihood">[glim:path-likelihood]</a>, and then projecting the terminal score onto the stopped filtration, gives $$0=\mathbb E_\Lambda[\dot F_{ij}+F_{ij}S_{ij}(s)]
   =\mathbb E_\Lambda[\dot F_{ij}+F_{ij}S_{ij}(\tau)].
 \label{glim:haar-identity}$$ Here is a justification at the stopping boundary. The stopping rule is constant on each rotation orbit of a fixed marked history, so $\dot F_{ij}$ differentiates only $x_i x_j$. At each fixed $n$ and spectrum, the likelihood is bounded by $2^N$, where $N$ is the number of rings, and its derivative is bounded by this quantity times a constant (depending on $n$ and the spectrum) times $N$. Poisson exponential moments justify differentiation of the full-time integral. The random variable $F_{ij}$ is measurable at $\tau$, and optional projection of the square-integrable martingale replaces $S_{ij}(s)$ by $S_{ij}(\tau)$. This proves <a href="#glim:haar-identity" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="glim:haar-identity">[glim:haar-identity]</a> without differentiating a law with a moving stopping time.

<a id="glim:individual-integral"></a>
Since $\dot x_i=x_j$ and $\dot x_j=-x_i$, this identity reads $$I_i-I_j=\mathbb E_\Lambda\!\left[
 S_{ij}(\tau)\int_0^\tau x_i(v)x_j(v)\,dv\right].$$ Sum over $j\le m$, $j\ne i$. The pathwise bound $$\sum_{\substack{j\le m\\j\ne i}}\left(\int_0^\tau x_i x_j\,dv\right)^2
 \le \left(\int_0^\tau x_i^2\,dv\right)
       \left(\int_0^\tau D_m\,dv\right)
 \le I\int_0^\tau x_i^2\,dv$$ and Cauchy–Schwarz on the product of probability and index spaces, together with $\sum_{j\le m} I_j\le I$ and <a href="#glim:rotation-score" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="glim:rotation-score">[glim:rotation-score]</a>, yield <a id="glim:integrated-rotation"></a>$$m I_i\le I+
 \left\{C m^{4/3}
       (m I_i+I+m s n^{-2/3})\,I I_i\right\}^{1/2}.
 \label{glim:integrated-rotation}$$ This estimate does not require independence between the scores. To solve it, put $$y=\frac{m I_i}{I},\qquad
 \alpha=C I m^{1/3},\qquad
 \kappa=\frac{m s n^{-2/3}}{I}.$$ It gives $y\le1+\sqrt{\alpha y(y+1+\kappa)}$. Here $I m^{1/3}=O(s^{4/75})$, while $\kappa\to0$ as $n\to\infty$ at each fixed $s$. For sufficiently small $s$ and then sufficiently large $n$, $\kappa\le1$ and $\sqrt\alpha\le1/2$. Using $\sqrt{y(y+2)}\le y+1$ proves $$I_i\le 3I/m\qquad(i\le m).
 \label{glim:individual-integral}$$

<a id="glim:one-mode"></a>
Repeat <a href="#glim:haar-identity" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="glim:haar-identity">[glim:haar-identity]</a> with $F_{ij}=\mathbf 1_G x_i(s)x_j(s)$. This random variable is measurable at $\tau$: it is zero if $\tau<s$, and otherwise is measurable at $s=\tau$. The indicator $G$, including its boundary, is constant on each rotation orbit, so its differentiation contributes nothing. Write $Z_a=\mathbb E_\Lambda[\mathbf 1_G x_a(s)^2]$ for $a\le m$. Now $\sum_{a\le m} Z_a\le R$ and $$\sum_{\substack{j\le m\\j\ne i}}\mathbb E_\Lambda[\mathbf 1_G x_i(s)^2x_j(s)^2]\le R Z_i.$$ Use <a href="#glim:rotation-score" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="glim:rotation-score">[glim:rotation-score]</a> and <a href="#glim:individual-integral" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="glim:individual-integral">[glim:individual-integral]</a> in the summed identity. Taking $n$ large enough that $m s n^{-2/3}\le I$, we obtain <a id="glim:terminal-rotation"></a>$$m Z_i\le R+\big(C m^{4/3} I R Z_i\big)^{1/2},
 \qquad Z_i\le C R/m.
 \label{glim:terminal-rotation}$$ For the second inequality, $z=mZ_i/R$ satisfies $z\le1+\sqrt{\alpha z}$, and hence $z\le2+\alpha$. As $R/m\le C s^{18/25}$, Markov’s inequality gives, at each of the retained spectra, $$\mathbb P_\Lambda\{x_i(s)^2>s^{13/20},\,G\}
 \le s^{-13/20}Z_i\le C s^{7/100}.
 \label{glim:one-mode}$$

We now combine the two probability laws. Let $\mathbb P_n$ include the Gaussian disorder, the independent diagonal and eigenvector signs, and the uniform-start dynamics. Write $\mathbb P_{\mathrm{dis}}$ and $\mathbb E_{\mathrm{dis}}$ for the completed disorder law and $\mathbb E_{\mathrm{eig}}$ for the eigenvalue law. Then $$\begin{aligned}
 \mathbb P_n\{x_i(s)^2>s^{13/20}\}
 \le{}&
 \mathbb P_{\mathrm{dis}}\big((\mathcal G_{n,\varepsilon}
                         \cap\mathcal S_{n,\varepsilon})^c\big)\\
 &+\mathbb E_{\mathrm{dis}}\!\left[
   \mathbf 1_{\mathcal G_{n,\varepsilon}\cap\mathcal S_{n,\varepsilon}}
                   \mathbb P_{\nu_n}^J(G^c)\right]\\
 &+\mathbb E_{\mathrm{eig}}\!\left[
   \mathbf 1_{\mathcal S_{n,\varepsilon}}
      \mathbb P_\Lambda\{x_i(s)^2>s^{13/20},G\}\right].
\end{aligned}$$ The second term uses <a href="#glim:cutoff-loss" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="glim:cutoff-loss">[glim:cutoff-loss]</a>; the last uses <a href="#glim:one-mode" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="glim:one-mode">[glim:one-mode]</a> with its full conditional Haar average. The complements of $\mathcal G_{n,\varepsilon}$ and $\mathcal S_{n,\varepsilon}$ cost at most $2\varepsilon$ in the limit, so for each fixed $i$ and all sufficiently small $s$, <a id="glim:finite-numerator"></a>$$\limsup_n\mathbb P_n\{x_i(s)^2>s^{13/20}\}
 \le2\varepsilon+
 C_\varepsilon\big(s^{17/150}+s^{1/60}+s^{7/100}\big).
 \label{glim:finite-numerator}$$ This separation is essential: no frame-dependent quenched event was imposed inside the Haar identity. Sending $s\downarrow0$ and then $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ proves the finite numerator estimate.

<a id="glim:limit-numerator"></a>
For a fixed positive $s$, the cylinder convergence in Proposition <a href="#prop:gaussian-subsequence" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:gaussian-subsequence">25</a> transfers this estimate to $\rho_s(dx)=h_s(x)\Pi_g(dx)$. Indeed each coordinate marginal of $\Pi_g$ has a density by (OpenAI 2026d, Proposition 2.3) <a id="pm-cite-95"></a>[[FUA](#ref-FUA)]; the same is true of $\rho_s$. The boundary $x_i^2=s^{13/20}$ thus has zero limiting probability. Weak convergence of this coordinate marginal and bounded convergence over the represented environment yield $$\lim_{s\downarrow0}
       \widehat{\mathbb E}\big[\rho_s\{x_i^2>s^{13/20}\}\big]=0.
 \label{glim:limit-numerator}$$ Only finite-coordinate convergence was used in this step.

<a id="pm-h-29"></a>
###### The weighted denominator.

Corollary <a href="#edge:limit-growth" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="edge:limit-growth">7</a> gives the two-sided bound in <a href="#glim:rates" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="glim:rates">[glim:rates]</a> for every admissible $b$, with measurable constants when $b$ is measurable. It remains to choose $b$ with $D_g(b)>0$. Start with a measurable admissible $b_0$, for example $b_0=1+(-g_1)_+$. The resolvent-difference identity in (OpenAI 2026d, Proposition 2.3) <a id="pm-cite-96"></a>[[FUA](#ref-FUA)] gives, for $b\ge b_0$, $$D_g(b)-D_g(b_0)=
 \sum_a\left(\frac1{g_a+b_0}-\frac1{g_a+b}\right).$$ The right side increases to $+\infty$ as $b\to\infty$, because $\sum_a(g_a+b_0)^{-1}=\infty$. Choose the first integer increment $b=b_0+j$ for which $D_g(b)>0$. This is measurable and admissible, so Corollary <a href="#edge:limit-growth" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="edge:limit-growth">7</a> gives <a href="#glim:rates" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="glim:rates">[glim:rates]</a>.

Put $\ell_a=r_a^{-1}$. The uniform coordinate moment bound in (OpenAI 2026d, Proposition 2.3) <a id="pm-cite-97"></a>[[FUA](#ref-FUA)] gives $$\Pi_g[M_g]\le C_g\sum_a\ell_a^2<\infty.$$ The first coordinate has no atom at zero, so $M_g>0$ almost surely. This proves that <a href="#glim:weighted-size" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="glim:weighted-size">[glim:weighted-size]</a> is well defined under $\Pi_g$ and under every $\rho_s$.

Let $N=\lceil s^{-8/5}\rceil$ and consider the coordinates $N\le a\le2N$. Under the independent Gaussian law of the conditioning construction, write $Z_a=\sqrt{\ell_a}\xi_a$ with independent standard normals $\xi_a$. Equation <a href="#glim:rates" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="glim:rates">[glim:rates]</a> implies $$\frac12\sum_{a=N}^{2N}\ell_a Z_a^2
 \ge c_gN^{-4/3}\sum_{a=N}^{2N}\xi_a^2.$$ The chi-square lower-tail bound shows that this is at least $c_gN^{-1/3}$, except on an event of probability at most $C_g e^{-c_gN}$.

<a id="glim:conditioned-tail-density"></a>
<a id="glim:denominator-static"></a>
The same estimate survives the norm conditioning with a fixed cost. Leave a sufficiently large fixed head of $m_0$ coordinates outside this block. Let $q$ be the density of $\sum_a(Z_a^2-\ell_a)$, and $q_{m_0}^{\rm head}$ the density of its first $m_0$ terms. The tail disintegration in (OpenAI 2026d, Proposition 2.3) <a id="pm-cite-98"></a>[[FUA](#ref-FUA)] states that $$\frac{d(\Pi_g)_{>m_0}}{d\bigotimes_{a>m_0}N(0,\ell_a)}
 =
 \frac{q_{m_0}^{\rm head}\!\left(
 D_g(b)-\sum_{a>m_0}(x_a^2-\ell_a)\right)}{q(D_g(b))}.
 \label{glim:conditioned-tail-density}$$ The head density is bounded by Fourier inversion once $m_0$ is large enough, and $q(D_g(b))>0$. Hence the ratio in <a href="#glim:conditioned-tail-density" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="glim:conditioned-tail-density">[glim:conditioned-tail-density]</a> is bounded by a finite $g$-dependent constant. For all sufficiently small $s$, the block lies outside the head and $$c_g N^{-1/3}\ge s^{14/25},
 \qquad\text{since}\qquad
 \frac{14}{25}-\frac8{15}=\frac2{75}>0.$$ It follows that $$\Pi_g\{M_g<s^{14/25}\}\le C_g e^{-c_g s^{-8/5}}.
 \label{glim:denominator-static}$$ Using <a href="#glim:density-family" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="glim:density-family">[glim:density-family]</a>, for almost every represented environment we obtain $$\rho_s\{M_g<s^{14/25}\}
 \le C_g C\exp\!\left(C s^{-77/50}-c_gs^{-8/5}\right)
 \longrightarrow0,$$ because $8/5>77/50$. These probabilities are bounded by one, so the convergence also holds after $\widehat{\mathbb E}$.

On the complement of the two exceptional events in <a href="#glim:limit-numerator" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="glim:limit-numerator">[glim:limit-numerator]</a> and <a href="#glim:denominator-static" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="glim:denominator-static">[glim:denominator-static]</a>, $$\frac{x_i^2}{M_g(x)}
 \le s^{13/20-14/25}=s^{9/100}.$$ This tends to zero and proves <a href="#glim:seed-escape" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="glim:seed-escape">[glim:seed-escape]</a>. ◻

</details>

For each represented limiting law, the averaged limit in <a href="#glim:seed-escape" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="glim:seed-escape">[glim:seed-escape]</a> yields a deterministic rational sequence $s_k\downarrow0$ along which, for almost every represented environment, the displayed conditional probabilities tend to zero for every fixed $i$ and $\epsilon>0$. Section <a href="#sec:entrance-selection" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:entrance-selection">6</a> proves this extraction and uses the resulting criterion.

<a id="sec:entrance-selection"></a>
### Selection of the entrance law

Proposition <a href="#prop:gaussian-subsequence" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:gaussian-subsequence">25</a> gives positive-time density families for the edge semigroup, but an extracted family might still depend on randomness beyond the edge points. The uniform-start estimate of Proposition <a href="#prop:uniform-seed-escape" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:uniform-seed-escape">26</a> is averaged over the represented environment. We first prove fixed-$g$ uniqueness from a sequential escape criterion and derive the zero-coordinate boundary from that criterion. We then extract a qualifying sequence for almost every represented environment and obtain a family measurable in $g$.

<a id="entr:rates"></a>
Fix $g$ in a common Borel full-measure subset of the edge set chosen in Proposition <a href="#prop:uniform-seed-escape" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:uniform-seed-escape">26</a> on which the conclusions about the conditioned law and the closed gradient form in Items 1 and 3 of Proposition <a href="#prop:stationary-inputs" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:stationary-inputs">2</a> hold with their stated source versions. The rate, finiteness, and positivity conclusions of Proposition <a href="#prop:uniform-seed-escape" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:uniform-seed-escape">26</a> hold on this set as well. In this section write $$r_i=g_i+b(g),\qquad D=D_g(b(g)),\qquad \Pi=\Pi_g,\qquad H=H_g.$$ Thus $D>0$, and there are constants $0<c_g<C_g<\infty$ such that $$\label{entr:rates}
 c_g(1+i)^{2/3}\le r_i\le C_g(1+i)^{2/3}\qquad(i\ge1).$$ Constants with a subscript $g$ below may be enlarged or decreased and depend only on this fixed realization, unless other dependencies are displayed. Recall the finite, strictly positive random variable <a id="entr:mass"></a>$$\label{entr:mass}
 M(x)=\sum_{i\ge1}\frac{x_i^2}{2r_i},\qquad x\sim\Pi.$$ Its finiteness follows from the uniform coordinate moment bound $\Pi[x_i^2]\le C_g/r_i$ and $\sum_i r_i^{-2}<\infty$; its positivity follows from the absolute continuity of a one-coordinate marginal. These properties of $\Pi$ are part of the conditioned edge law (OpenAI 2026d, Proposition 2.3) <a id="pm-cite-99"></a>[[FUA](#ref-FUA)].

<a id="stmt-thm-entrance-selection"></a>
<div id="thm:entrance-selection" class="theorem">

**Theorem 27** (Entrance selection). *For every $g$ as above, there is at most one family $(h_s)_{s>0}$ of probability densities with respect to $\Pi_g$ with the following properties:*

1.  *$h_s\ge0$, $\Pi_g[h_s]=1$, and $\sup_{s_0\le s\le s_1}\|h_s\|_{L^\infty(\Pi_g)}<\infty$ whenever $0<s_0<s_1<\infty$;*

2.  *$h_{s+t}=S_t^g h_s$ in $L^2(\Pi_g)$ for $s,t>0$, where $S_t^g=\exp(-t c_*H_g)$;*

<a id="entr:escape"></a>
3.  *there is a sequence $s_k\downarrow0$ such that, for every $i\ge1$ and $\varepsilon>0$, $$\label{entr:escape}
     \Pi_g\left[h_{s_k}\,
           \mathbf 1_{\{x_i^2/M(x)>\varepsilon\}}\right]\longrightarrow0.$$*

<a id="entr:zero-boundary"></a>
*Any such family satisfies $$\label{entr:zero-boundary}
 h_s\Pi_g\ \Longrightarrow\ \delta_{\boldsymbol 0}
 \quad\text{on \(\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}\) with its product topology, as \(s\downarrow0\)}.$$ For almost every $g$ such a family exists. It can be chosen measurably in $g$, as a family of $L^2(\Pi_g)$ density classes, and with jointly measurable density representatives in $(g,s,x)$. Every represented Gaussian limit in Proposition <a href="#prop:gaussian-subsequence" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:gaussian-subsequence">25</a> is this family almost surely.*

</div>

The hypothesis <a href="#entr:escape" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="entr:escape">[entr:escape]</a> describes information retained from the finite uniform initialization. Different candidate families may use different sequences in Item 3. The zero-coordinate limit <a href="#entr:zero-boundary" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="entr:zero-boundary">[entr:zero-boundary]</a> is a consequence of that hypothesis and holds as $s$ decreases to zero through all positive times.

<a id="entr:unit-time"></a>
We prove uniqueness in the time variable $$\label{entr:unit-time}
 u=c_*s,\qquad \widetilde h_u=h_{u/c_*},\qquad
 \widetilde S_u=e^{-uH}.$$ Then $\widetilde h_{u+v}=\widetilde S_v\widetilde h_u$. The sequence $u_k=c_*s_k$ has exactly the escape property <a href="#entr:escape" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="entr:escape">[entr:escape]</a>. All elapsed times in the next three subsections refer to $\widetilde S$. We return to $s=u/c_*$ at the end.

<a id="pm-h-31"></a>
#### Angular coordinates and a common diffusion factor

We need a stochastic realization only after a positive time, where the initial law has a bounded density. Put $m=12$ and define $$R(x)=\left(\sum_{j\le m}x_j^2\right)^{1/2}.$$ On $\{R>0\}$, set $$\theta_i(x)=\frac{x_i}{R(x)},\qquad
 \overline r(x)=\sum_{j\le m}r_j\theta_j(x)^2 .$$ The functions $\theta_i$ are homogeneous of degree zero: if a finite set $J$ contains the head $\{1,\ldots,m\}$ and $i$, then $\sum_{j\in J}x_j\partial_j\theta_i=0$. In the finite-coordinate density of $\Pi$, the factor imposing the square constraint has a radial derivative. Its contribution to the generator therefore vanishes on $\theta_i$. The next lemma justifies this cancellation for the associated diffusion, including avoidance of $R=0$.

<a id="stmt-entr-angular-realization"></a>
<div id="entr:angular-realization" class="lemma">

<a id="entr:angular-sde"></a>
**Lemma 28** (Angular realization). *Let $w$ be a bounded probability density with respect to $\Pi$. There is a continuous process $X(t)=(X_i(t))_{i\ge1}$ on $\mathbb R^\mathbb N$, with law $(\widetilde S_t w)\Pi$ at time $t$, and independent standard Brownian motions $(W_i)_{i\ge1}$ in its filtration, with the following property. Almost surely $R(X(t))>0$ for all $t\ge0$. With $R(t)=R(X(t))$, $\Theta_i(t)=\theta_i(X(t))$, and $\overline r(t)=\overline r(X(t))$, one has $$\begin{aligned}
 d\Theta_i(t)
 &=
 \frac{\sqrt2}{R(t)}
 \left(dW_i(t)-\Theta_i(t)\sum_{j\le m}\Theta_j(t)\,dW_j(t)\right)
 \notag\\
 &\quad+
 \Theta_i(t)\left(
  \frac{3-m-2\mathbf 1_{\{i\le m\}}}{R(t)^2}-r_i+\overline r(t)
 \right)dt .                                      \label{entr:angular-sde}
\end{aligned}$$ All identities hold simultaneously for $i\ge1$. The Brownian increments after zero are independent of the initial sigma field.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-entr-angular-realization"><summary>Proof of stmt-entr-angular-realization</summary>

*Proof.* The closed form of $H$ is $\mathcal E_g(F,G)=\Pi[\nabla F\cdot\nabla G]$. Its domain is the closure of the smooth compact cylinder functions, contains the constants and all coordinates, and satisfies $\nabla x_i=e_i$ (OpenAI 2026d, Proposition 5.1) <a id="pm-cite-100"></a>[[FUA](#ref-FUA)]. Smooth contractions on the core extend by closure, so this is a Dirichlet form. The same approximation, with smooth clipping to preserve a common bound, gives the chain and bounded product rules. In particular the gradient vanishes almost everywhere on a set on which the function is constant: apply the chain rule to smooth truncations in successively smaller neighborhoods of the constant, and use closedness. These rules show strong locality.

Here are the topological hypotheses for the diffusion theorem. The state space $\mathbb R^\mathbb N$ is Polish in the product topology. The smooth compact cylinder core consists of continuous functions and contains a countable family separating its points. To obtain a compact nest, for each coordinate choose a smooth function $v_j$, equal to one outside a sufficiently large coordinate interval and zero on a smaller interval, with $\|v_j\|_{\mathcal E_g,1}\le\epsilon2^{-j}$. Such a choice is possible: coordinate tails have vanishing $\Pi$-mass, while a transition of increasing width makes the gradient norm vanish. The sum $\sum_jv_j$ converges in the form norm and is at least one on the complement of a compact product box. The definition of $1$-capacity therefore bounds that complement’s capacity by $\epsilon^2$. Taking $\epsilon\downarrow0$ and enlarging successive boxes gives a compact nest. The form is thus quasi-regular. Since $1$ has zero energy, its semigroup fixes $1$; the associated process has infinite lifetime under $\Pi$, and hence under $w\Pi$.

The diffusion theorem and locality criterion for quasi-regular symmetric Dirichlet forms now give a continuous associated process (Ma and Röckner 1992, Theorems IV.3.5 and V.1.11) <a id="pm-cite-101"></a>[[MaRockner](#ref-MaRockner)]. Its Fukushima decomposition is supplied by (Ma and Röckner 1992, Theorem VI.2.5) <a id="pm-cite-102"></a>[[MaRockner](#ref-MaRockner)]. In particular, the coordinate martingales $M^i$ are continuous and have brackets $$\langle M^i,M^j\rangle_t
   =2\int_0^t \nabla x_i\cdot\nabla x_j(X(v))\,dv
   =2\delta_{ij}t.$$ The bracket identity is the energy-measure identity for the form, given by (Fukushima, Oshima, and Takeda 2011, Theorem 5.2.3 and Equation (5.2.34)) <a id="pm-cite-103"></a>[[FOT](#ref-FOT)] after the quasi-regular regularization of (Ma and Röckner 1992, chap. VI) <a id="pm-cite-104"></a>[[MaRockner](#ref-MaRockner)]. To apply its bounded formula, first take a bounded smooth clip $u_N=c_N(x_i)$. For every bounded form-domain test $f$, the chain and product rules give $$2\mathcal E_g(u_Nf,u_N)-\mathcal E_g(u_N^2,f)
       =2\Pi[f|c_N'(x_i)|^2].$$ Choose the clips with $|c_N'|\le1$ and $c_N(x_i)\to x_i$ in form norm. Passing to the limit in the energy measures and polarizing gives the displayed coordinate brackets. The multidimensional Lévy characterization, for every finite set of indices, gives $M^i=\sqrt2W_i$ with the asserted countable family of Brownian motions. Brownian motion here is relative to the filtration of the process, so its future increments are independent of the initial sigma field. The usual form exceptional set has $\Pi$-measure zero; it can be discarded for $w\Pi$. These facts also give continuous coordinate paths.

<a id="entr:cylinder-density"></a>
We verify the generator used for $\theta_i$. The finite-coordinate density formula for $\Pi$, on any finite set $J$, is $$\label{entr:cylinder-density}
 \frac{q_{J^c}\!\left(D-\sum_{j\in J}(x_j^2-r_j^{-1})\right)}
      {q(D)}
 \prod_{j\in J}\left(\frac{r_j}{2\pi}\right)^{1/2}
                     e^{-r_jx_j^2/2}.$$ Here $q$ is the density of the full centered Gaussian square sum, and $q_{J^c}$ is the density after the coordinates in $J$ are deleted (OpenAI 2026d, Proposition 2.3) <a id="pm-cite-105"></a>[[FUA](#ref-FUA)]. Both densities exist, $q(D)>0$, and $q_{J^c}$ has bounded derivatives of any prescribed finite order. For the last assertion, leave sufficiently many fixed indices outside $J$; the product of their characteristic-function moduli is bounded by $\prod (1+4t^2r_j^{-2})^{-1/4}$, which is integrable even after multiplication by the prescribed power of $|t|$. Fourier inversion then gives the assertion. In particular <a href="#entr:cylinder-density" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="entr:cylinder-density">[entr:cylinder-density]</a> is bounded by a constant times the product Gaussian density.

The set $R=0$ is polar. Indeed a smooth cutoff equal to one on $\{R\le\epsilon\}$, zero on $\{R\ge2\epsilon\}$, and with derivative $O(\epsilon^{-1})$, has squared form norm $O(\epsilon^m+\epsilon^{m-2})$, by <a href="#entr:cylinder-density" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="entr:cylinder-density">[entr:cylinder-density]</a>. Letting $\epsilon\downarrow0$ proves zero capacity. A diffusion starting outside its exceptional set never hits a polar set, which proves the stated pathwise positivity of $R$.

For a cylinder test whose index set $J$ contains $\{1,\ldots,m,i\}$, integrate by parts in <a href="#entr:cylinder-density" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="entr:cylinder-density">[entr:cylinder-density]</a>. The derivative of the factor $q_{J^c}$ is radial in the $J$ coordinates. Its pairing with the gradient of $\theta_i$ vanishes, because $\sum_{j\in J}x_j\partial_j\theta_i=0$. Consequently the nonpositive generator on this function is $$\mathcal L\theta_i=\Delta\theta_i-\sum_{j\in J}r_jx_j\partial_j\theta_i.$$ This integration by parts is legitimate across $R=0$. More explicitly, cut off at $R=\epsilon$ and at large finite-coordinate radius. The function and its first two derivatives near zero are bounded by $C_i(1+|x_i|)(1+R^{-3})$. The products with derivatives of the scale-$\epsilon$ cutoff satisfy the same bound on $R\asymp\epsilon$. Their squared integrals near zero vanish for $m=12>6$. Terms with a derivative on $q_{J^c}$ are bounded by the same Gaussian integrals with polynomial factors, since its first derivative is bounded. Gaussian tails handle the outer cutoff. Thus the cutoffs converge in the form norm, proving $\theta_i$ belongs to the form domain, and the weak generator pairing passes to the limit. The displayed $\mathcal L\theta_i$ is in $L^2(\Pi)$ by the same bounds. Extending the pairing from the core shows $\theta_i\in\operatorname{Dom}(H)$ and $H\theta_i=-\mathcal L\theta_i$.

A direct differentiation gives, with the head vector extended by zeros, $$\partial_j\theta_i=\frac{\delta_{ij}-\theta_i\theta_j\mathbf 1_{\{j\le m\}}}{R},
 \qquad
 \mathcal L\theta_i
 =\theta_i\left(\frac{3-m-2\mathbf 1_{\{i\le m\}}}{R^2}
                         -r_i+\overline r\right).$$ The Fukushima drift is the time integral of this $L^2$ generator. Its martingale has brackets with the coordinate martingales equal to $2\int_0^t\partial_j\theta_i(X(v))\,dv$, and self-bracket $2\int_0^t|\nabla\theta_i(X(v))|^2\,dv$. It therefore equals $\sqrt2\sum_j\int_0^t\partial_j\theta_i(X(v))\,dW_j(v)$: the difference has zero bracket. Only the head and index $i$ occur in this finite sum. Integrability follows, for instance, from $$\mathbb E\int_0^T|\nabla\theta_i(X(v))|^2\,dv
 \le T\|w\|_\infty\mathcal E_g(\theta_i)<\infty,$$ because $\|\widetilde S_vw\|_\infty\le\|w\|_\infty$. This proves <a href="#entr:angular-sde" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="entr:angular-sde">[entr:angular-sde]</a>. Countability permits a common null set for all indices. ◻

</details>

<a id="entr:scalar-rescaling"></a>
<a id="entr:YQ"></a>
<a id="entr:common-sde"></a>
<a id="entr:seed-weights"></a>
We now cancel the common head projection in the angular martingale and the common angular drift with a single stochastic integrating factor. On the process of Lemma <a href="#entr:angular-realization" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="entr:angular-realization">28</a>, define the positive scalar $\mathcal U(t)$ by $$\label{entr:scalar-rescaling}
 \mathcal U(0)=\frac{R(0)}{\sqrt{M(X(0))}},\qquad
 d\mathcal U
 =\mathcal U\left\{
     \frac{\sqrt2}{R}\sum_{j\le m}\Theta_j\,dW_j
       +\left(\frac{m-1}{R^2}-\overline r\right)dt\right\}.$$ This is the stochastic exponential with the displayed drift and initial value. On every compact time interval $R$ has a strictly positive minimum, so all its coefficients are locally bounded along the path; the exponential is finite and strictly positive. Put $$\label{entr:YQ}
 Q=\frac{\mathcal U}{R},\qquad f=Q^2,\qquad
 Y_i=\mathcal U\Theta_i=QX_i,\qquad y_i=Y_i(0).$$ In the product rule for $\mathcal U\Theta_i$, the quadratic covariation contributes $2\mathcal U\Theta_i(\mathbf 1_{\{i\le m\}}-1)R^{-2}dt$. Adding this to the two drifts in <a href="#entr:angular-sde" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="entr:angular-sde">[entr:angular-sde]</a>–<a href="#entr:scalar-rescaling" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="entr:scalar-rescaling">[entr:scalar-rescaling]</a> cancels all terms containing $R^{-2}$ or $\overline r$. Their martingale terms cancel the head projection. Thus $$\label{entr:common-sde}
 dY_i=-r_iY_i\,dt+\sqrt2Q\,dW_i,\qquad
 Y_i(t)=e^{-r_it}y_i+\sqrt2\int_0^t e^{-r_i(t-v)}Q(v)\,dW_i(v).$$ Both $Q$ and $f$ are positive continuous processes, including at elapsed time zero. The normalization at zero gives $$\label{entr:seed-weights}
 p_i:=\frac{y_i^2}{2r_i}\ge0,\qquad
 \sum_i p_i=1,\qquad
 y_i^2=\frac{X_i(0)^2}{M(X(0))}.$$ In particular <a href="#entr:escape" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="entr:escape">[entr:escape]</a> says that these weights leave every finite set in probability when the starting time decreases along its specified sequence.

<a id="pm-h-32"></a>
#### The scalar constraint equation

<a id="entr:finite-constraint"></a>
The coordinates in <a href="#entr:common-sde" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="entr:common-sde">[entr:common-sde]</a> are driven by the same factor $Q$. The quadratic constraint on $X$ determines that factor through a scalar Volterra equation. To identify the equation before taking an infinite limit, view $f$ and the time kernels causally, by extending them by zero to negative elapsed times, and fix $N$. Set $$E_i(t)=e^{-2r_it}\quad(t\ge0),\qquad
 L_N(t)=\sum_{i\le N}r_i^{-1}E_i(t),\qquad
 R_N(x)=D-\sum_{i\le N}(x_i^2-r_i^{-1}).$$ Itô’s formula in <a href="#entr:common-sde" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="entr:common-sde">[entr:common-sde]</a> gives $$Y_i(t)^2=E_i(t)y_i^2+2(E_i*f)(t)
       +2\sqrt2\int_0^t E_i(t-v)Q(v)Y_i(v)\,dW_i(v).$$ Since $\sum_{i\le N}Y_i^2=f\sum_{i\le N}X_i^2$ and $$\sum_{i\le N}X_i^2
   =D+\sum_{i\le N}r_i^{-1}-R_N(X),$$ rearrangement gives, as an identity of causal distributions, $$\label{entr:finite-constraint}
 Df+(L_N*f)'=
 \sum_{i\le N}E_i y_i^2
 +2\sqrt2\sum_{i\le N} E_i*(QY_i\,dW_i)+fR_N(X).$$ Here the derivative includes the mass at elapsed time zero: <a id="entr:initial-delta"></a>$$\label{entr:initial-delta}
 L_N'=\left(\sum_{i\le N}r_i^{-1}\right)\delta_0
                       -2\sum_{i\le N}E_i .$$ Thus the coefficient of $f$ contributed by the delta mass is retained in <a href="#entr:finite-constraint" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="entr:finite-constraint">[entr:finite-constraint]</a>. This identity is exact for finite $N$. The remaining passage must remove $fR_N(X)$ and replace $L_N$ by $$L(t)=\sum_i r_i^{-1}E_i(t),\qquad t>0.$$ The corresponding limiting operator on $f$ is convolution with $D\delta_0+L'$. The next lemma constructs its positive inverse kernel and the bounds needed for the stochastic terms.

<a id="stmt-entr-kernels"></a>
<div id="entr:kernels" class="lemma">

<a id="entr:K-bounds"></a>
<a id="entr:Ki-bounds"></a>
<a id="entr:Ki-limit"></a>
<a id="entr:Ki-sup"></a>
<a id="entr:Ki-sum"></a>
<a id="entr:Ki-increment"></a>
<a id="entr:kernel-inverse"></a>
**Lemma 29** (Resolvent kernels). *For $L$ defined above, let $$\widehat K(z)=\frac{1}{D+z\widehat L(z)}\quad(z>0),$$ where a hat denotes the Laplace transform and every kernel is zero on negative times. The function $L$ is locally integrable, and $\widehat K$ is the Laplace transform of a nonnegative, decreasing function $K$, smooth on $(0,\infty)$. For $0<t\le1$, $$\label{entr:K-bounds}
 c_g t^{-1/2}\le K(t)\le C_g t^{-1/2},
 \qquad |K'(t)|\le C_g t^{-3/2}.$$ Set $K_i=K*E_i$. Then $$\begin{aligned}
 K_i(t)&\le C_g\frac{\sqrt t}{1+r_it},&
 |K_i'(t)|&\le C_g\frac{t^{-1/2}}{1+r_it},             \label{entr:Ki-bounds}\\
 2r_iK_i(t)&\longrightarrow K(t)                       \label{entr:Ki-limit}
\end{aligned}$$ uniformly on each compact subinterval of $(0,1]$ as $i\to\infty$. For $t>0$, $h\ge0$, $t+h\le1$, and $0\le\xi<1/4$, $$\begin{aligned}
 \sup_i r_iK_i(t)^2&\le C_g,&
 \sup_i r_i|K_i(t+h)-K_i(t)|^2
   &\le C_g\min\{1,h^2/t^2\},                          \label{entr:Ki-sup}\\
 \sum_i(1+r_i)^{2\xi}K_i(t)^2
   &\le C_{g,\xi}t^{-1/2-2\xi},                       \label{entr:Ki-sum}\\
 \sum_i|K_i(t+h)-K_i(t)|^2
   &\le C_g t^{-1/2}\min\{1,h^2/t^2\}.                \label{entr:Ki-increment}
\end{aligned}$$ As causal distributions, $$\label{entr:kernel-inverse}
 K*(D\delta_0+L')=\delta_0.$$*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-entr-kernels"><summary>Proof of stmt-entr-kernels</summary>

*Proof.* The local integrability follows directly from $$\int_0^T L(t)\,dt
 =\frac12\sum_i r_i^{-2}(1-e^{-2r_iT})<\infty.$$ For $L_N=\sum_{i\le N}r_i^{-1}E_i$, put $$F_N(z)=D+z\widehat L_N(z)
       =D+\sum_{i\le N}\frac{z}{r_i(z+2r_i)}.$$ The rational function $F_N$ is strictly increasing between its negative poles, since $F_N'(z)=\sum_{i\le N}2(z+2r_i)^{-2}>0$. Its zeros interlace those poles and are strictly negative, using $D>0$. Its reciprocal is therefore a positive constant plus a sum of positive multiples of $(z+a)^{-1}$, $a>0$: the residue at a zero is $1/F_N'(-a)>0$. Repeated rates can be grouped before this argument.

<a id="entr:laplace-scale"></a>
Write these sums as Stieltjes transforms of positive measures. Their measures weighted by $(1+a)^{-1}$, with the constant as mass at the point at infinity, have total mass $F_N(1)^{-1}\le D^{-1}$. Weak compactness on $[0,\infty]$ and monotone convergence of $F_N(z)$ give $$\frac1{D+z\widehat L(z)}
   =c+\int_{[0,\infty)}\frac{\nu(da)}{z+a},
 \qquad \int\frac{\nu(da)}{1+a}<\infty.$$ By <a href="#entr:rates" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="entr:rates">[entr:rates]</a>, splitting the sum at $r_i=z$ gives $$\label{entr:laplace-scale}
 D+z\widehat L(z)\asymp_g \sqrt z\qquad(z\ge1).$$ For sufficiently large $z$, the part with $r_i\le z$ is comparable to $\sum_{r_i\le z}r_i^{-1}\asymp\sqrt z$, and the other part to $z\sum_{r_i>z}r_i^{-2}\asymp\sqrt z$. Positivity and continuity adjust the constants on the remaining compact interval $z\ge1$. Hence the transform tends to zero at infinity and $c=0$. It is bounded as $z\downarrow0$, so $\nu$ has no atom at zero. The function $$K(t)=\int_{(0,\infty)}e^{-at}\nu(da)$$ has the required Laplace transform by Tonelli’s theorem. The weighted integrability of $\nu$ implies smoothness for $t>0$, and the representation makes $K$ positive and decreasing.

The upper bound in <a href="#entr:K-bounds" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="entr:K-bounds">[entr:K-bounds]</a> follows from $$e^{-1}tK(t)\le\int_0^t e^{-v/t}K(v)\,dv
 \le\widehat K(1/t)\le C_g\sqrt t.$$ For the lower bound choose a fixed small $\eta>0$. When $t\le\eta$, <a href="#entr:laplace-scale" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="entr:laplace-scale">[entr:laplace-scale]</a> bounds $\widehat K(\eta/t)$ below by $c_g\sqrt{t/\eta}$, whereas the upper bound just proved bounds its integral over $[0,t]$ by $C_g\sqrt t$. Choose $\eta$ so that the first constant is larger than twice the second. The integral over $[t,\infty)$ is at most $\eta^{-1}t e^{-\eta}K(t)$, proving the lower bound for $t\le\eta$. Positivity and monotonicity adjust the constant on $[\eta,1]$. Finally $$|K'(t)|=\int a e^{-at}\nu(da)
 \le \frac{C}{t}K(t/2)\le C_g t^{-3/2}.$$

For $r_it\le1$, integration of $K(v)\le C_gv^{-1/2}$ gives the first bound in <a href="#entr:Ki-bounds" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="entr:Ki-bounds">[entr:Ki-bounds]</a>. For $r_it>1$, write $K_i(t)=\int_0^t K(t-v)e^{-2r_iv}\,dv$ and split at $t/2$. The first half is bounded by $C_g/(r_i\sqrt t)$; the second by $C_g\sqrt t\,e^{-r_it}$, which has the same bound. For the derivative use $K_i'=K-2r_iK_i$. When $r_it\le1$ the preceding bounds suffice. When $r_it>1$, write $$K_i'(t)=K(t)e^{-2r_it}
  -2r_i\int_0^t e^{-2r_iv}\bigl(K(t-v)-K(t)\bigr)\,dv.$$ On $v\le t/2$ the derivative bound on $K$ makes the integrand difference at most $C_g v t^{-3/2}$; on $v>t/2$ the exponential factor pays the integral of $K$. This gives $|K_i'(t)|\le C_g/(r_it^{3/2})$. It also proves <a href="#entr:Ki-limit" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="entr:Ki-limit">[entr:Ki-limit]</a>, uniformly away from zero.

The remaining estimates follow by summing <a href="#entr:Ki-bounds" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="entr:Ki-bounds">[entr:Ki-bounds]</a>. For example <a href="#entr:rates" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="entr:rates">[entr:rates]</a> gives $$\sum_i\frac{(1+r_i)^{2\xi}}{(1+r_it)^2}
 \le C_{g,\xi}t^{-3/2-2\xi}\quad(0\le\xi<1/4).$$ The restriction on $\xi$ is exactly integrability at infinity after the change of variable $v=r_it$: the comparison integral there is $\int_0^\infty v^{1/2+2\xi}(1+v)^{-2}\,dv$. This proves <a href="#entr:Ki-sum" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="entr:Ki-sum">[entr:Ki-sum]</a>. If $h<t$, integrate the bound on $K_i'$ between $t$ and $t+h$, and then use the same sum with $\xi=0$; this gives <a href="#entr:Ki-increment" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="entr:Ki-increment">[entr:Ki-increment]</a> and <a href="#entr:Ki-sup" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="entr:Ki-sup">[entr:Ki-sup]</a>. If $h\ge t$, bound the two values separately. Finally the locally integrable function $$D\int_0^tK(v)\,dv+(K*L)(t)$$ has Laplace transform $1/z$, and hence equals $1$ for almost every $t>0$. Its causal distributional derivative gives <a href="#entr:kernel-inverse" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="entr:kernel-inverse">[entr:kernel-inverse]</a>. ◻

</details>

For the normalized seed weights $p_i=y_i^2/(2r_i)$, define, for $0<t\le1$, the candidate seed response $$A_y(t)=\sum_iK_i(t)y_i^2=\sum_i p_i\,2r_iK_i(t).$$ The bound $2r_iK_i(t)\le C_g t^{-1/2}$, together with $\sum_i p_i=1$, proves that this series converges uniformly on each compact subinterval of $(0,1]$. Its sum $A_y$ is continuous there and satisfies $0\le A_y(t)\le C_g t^{-1/2}$. The high-index limit $2r_iK_i\to K$ is the ingredient used below to prove $A_y\to K$ in probability, uniformly on compact subintervals of $(0,1]$, when the weights leave every fixed finite set. The bound $K(t)\asymp_g t^{-1/2}$ determines the scale used in the later stopped comparison of $f=Q^2$. The next lemma defines the infinite stochastic convolution and controls it uniformly over normalized seeds under the corresponding upper bound $|q(t)|\le C_0t^{-1/4}$.

<a id="stmt-entr-stochastic-kernels"></a>
<div id="entr:stochastic-kernels" class="lemma">

<a id="entr:Z-moment"></a>
<a id="entr:stoch-moment"></a>
<a id="entr:stoch-increment"></a>
**Lemma 30** (Stochastic kernel bounds). *Let $(W_i)$ be independent Brownian motions in a filtration, let $(y_i)$ be measurable at time zero with $\sum_i y_i^2/(2r_i)=1$, and let $q$ be progressively measurable with $|q(v)|\le C_0v^{-1/4}$ for $0<v\le1$. Define <a id="entr:stochastic-parts"></a>$$\begin{aligned}
 Z_i^q(t)&=\sqrt2\int_0^t e^{-r_i(t-v)}q(v)\,dW_i(v),\notag\\
 \mathsf G_q^y(t)&=2\sqrt2\sum_i\int_0^t
                K_i(t-v)q(v)e^{-r_iv}y_i\,dW_i(v),\label{entr:stochastic-parts}\\
 \mathsf N_q(t)&=2\sqrt2\sum_i\int_0^t
                K_i(t-v)q(v)Z_i^q(v)\,dW_i(v).\notag
\end{aligned}$$ The two series converge in probability in $C([0,1])$, with value zero at zero. For every finite $j\ge2$, their partial sums and their limits satisfy $$\begin{aligned}
 \|Z_i^q(t)\|_{L^j}^2
     &\le C_{g,C_0,j}\frac{\sqrt t}{1+r_it},           \label{entr:Z-moment}\\
 \|\mathsf G_q^y(t)\|_{L^j}+\|\mathsf N_q(t)\|_{L^j}
     &\le C_{g,C_0,j}t^{1/4},                         \label{entr:stoch-moment}\\
 \|\mathsf G_q^y(t+h)-\mathsf G_q^y(t)\|_{L^j}
  +\|\mathsf N_q(t+h)-\mathsf N_q(t)\|_{L^j}
     &\le C_{g,C_0,j}h^{1/4}\quad(0\le t<t+h\le1).
                                                               \label{entr:stoch-increment}
\end{aligned}$$ The supremum on $[0,1]$ of either limit has every finite moment, bounded by a constant depending only on $g,C_0$, and that order.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-entr-stochastic-kernels"><summary>Proof of stmt-entr-stochastic-kernels</summary>

*Proof.* The bracket estimate and the Burkholder–Davis–Gundy inequality give $$\|Z_i^q(t)\|_{L^j}^2
 \le C_{C_0,j}\int_0^t e^{-2r_i(t-v)}v^{-1/2}\,dv
 \le C_{C_0,j}\frac{\sqrt t}{1+r_it}.$$ For the last inequality split at $t/2$; on the second half use $v^{-1/2}\le C t^{-1/2}$, and on the first use $e^{-2r_i(t-v)}\le e^{-r_it}$.

Write $p_i=y_i^2/(2r_i)$. The bracket of the first series, at a fixed time $t$, is bounded pathwise by $$C_{C_0}\int_0^t v^{-1/2}
       \sum_i p_i r_iK_i(t-v)^2\,dv
 \le C_{g,C_0}\sqrt t,$$ by <a href="#entr:Ki-sup" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="entr:Ki-sup">[entr:Ki-sup]</a> and $\sum_i p_i=1$. This proves its bound in <a href="#entr:stoch-moment" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="entr:stoch-moment">[entr:stoch-moment]</a>. In its increment, the old portion of the bracket is at most $$C_{g,C_0}\int_0^t v^{-1/2}
              \min\{1,h^2/(t-v)^2\}\,dv
 \le C_{g,C_0}\sqrt h ,$$ and the new portion is bounded by $C\int_t^{t+h}v^{-1/2}\,dv\le C\sqrt h$. For the displayed integral, if $t\le2h$ discard the minimum; if $t>2h$, split at $t-h$ and at $t/2$. These bounds prove the first increment estimate.

For the second series, the martingale moment inequality followed by Minkowski’s inequality bounds its $L^j$ norm squared by $$C_j\int_0^t\sum_i K_i(t-v)^2
                      \|q(v)Z_i^q(v)\|_{L^j}^2\,dv
 \le C_{g,C_0,j}\int_0^t (t-v)^{-1/2}\,dv
 \le C_{g,C_0,j}\sqrt t.$$ We used <a href="#entr:Z-moment" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="entr:Z-moment">[entr:Z-moment]</a>, the deterministic bound on $q$, and <a href="#entr:Ki-sum" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="entr:Ki-sum">[entr:Ki-sum]</a> with $\xi=0$. For the increment use <a href="#entr:Ki-increment" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="entr:Ki-increment">[entr:Ki-increment]</a> on the old portion: its squared norm is bounded by $$C_{g,C_0,j}\int_0^t (t-v)^{-1/2}
                \min\{1,h^2/(t-v)^2\}\,dv
 \le C_{g,C_0,j}\sqrt h .$$ The new portion has the same bound by integrating $(t+h-v)^{-1/2}$ from $t$ to $t+h$.

All these estimates hold for partial sums. At each fixed time their tails tend to zero in $L^j$: for the first series use $\sum_{i>N}p_i r_iK_i(t-v)^2\to0$ and its constant bound inside the bracket; for the second use the summable bound just displayed. Dominated convergence applies in both cases. Taking $j>4$, <a href="#entr:stoch-increment" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="entr:stoch-increment">[entr:stoch-increment]</a> gives uniformly small moduli of continuity, by a dyadic chaining estimate (equivalently the Kolmogorov continuity criterion). Fixed-time convergence on a finite grid then proves convergence in probability in $C([0,1])$. The same chaining has a convergent series $\sum_{k\ge0}2^{k/j}2^{-k/4}$, and bounds the $L^j$ norm of the supremum for $j>4$. Taking a higher order gives the asserted bound for every finite order. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-entr-volterra"></a>
<div id="entr:volterra" class="lemma">

<a id="entr:volterra-equation"></a>
**Lemma 31** (The renormalized Volterra equation). *Let the processes be as in <a href="#entr:YQ" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="entr:YQ">[entr:YQ]</a>–<a href="#entr:common-sde" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="entr:common-sde">[entr:common-sde]</a>, and let $A_y$ be the candidate seed response defined above. Almost surely, for $0<t\le1$, $$\label{entr:volterra-equation}
 f(t)=A_y(t)+2\sqrt2\sum_i\int_0^t
               K_i(t-v)Q(v)Y_i(v)\,dW_i(v).$$ The stochastic series is defined by localization and has a continuous version on every compact subinterval of $(0,1]$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-entr-volterra"><summary>Proof of stmt-entr-volterra</summary>

<a id="entr:tail-residual"></a>
*Proof.* We now justify the infinite passage in <a href="#entr:finite-constraint" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="entr:finite-constraint">[entr:finite-constraint]</a>. The constraint says $R_N(x)=\sum_{i>N}(x_i^2-r_i^{-1})$ $\Pi$-almost surely. The conditioned edge law describes the tail, after any sufficiently large fixed head, by a bounded density relative to its product Gaussian law (OpenAI 2026d, Proposition 2.3) <a id="pm-cite-106"></a>[[FUA](#ref-FUA)]. Consequently, for $N$ beyond that head, $$\label{entr:tail-residual}
 \Pi[|R_N|]\le C_g\left(\sum_{i>N}r_i^{-2}\right)^{1/2}
       \longrightarrow0.$$ Indeed the Gaussian tail is centered and has variance $2\sum_{i>N}r_i^{-2}$.

<a id="entr:L-tail"></a>
The density of $X(t)$ is bounded by $\|w\|_\infty$ for all elapsed $t\ge0$. The constraint therefore holds for almost every elapsed time almost surely, and <a href="#entr:tail-residual" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="entr:tail-residual">[entr:tail-residual]</a> gives $$\mathbb E\int_0^T|R_N(X(v))|\,dv
       \le T\|w\|_\infty\Pi[|R_N|]\longrightarrow0 .$$ The continuous process $f$ is bounded on $[0,T]$ almost surely. First restrict to a bound for that supremum, and then let the bound increase. It follows that $fR_N(X)\to0$ in probability in $L^1(0,T)$. Also $$\label{entr:L-tail}
 \|L-L_N\|_{L^1(0,T)}
 \le\frac12\sum_{i>N}r_i^{-2}\longrightarrow0 .$$ Convolving <a href="#entr:finite-constraint" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="entr:finite-constraint">[entr:finite-constraint]</a> with $K$, its left side therefore tends to $f$ in local distributions by <a href="#entr:kernel-inverse" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="entr:kernel-inverse">[entr:kernel-inverse]</a>. One can see this directly by writing the difference as the derivative of $K*(L_N-L)*f$; its undifferentiated factor tends to zero in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ by <a href="#entr:L-tail" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="entr:L-tail">[entr:L-tail]</a>. The convolved residual also tends to zero in probability in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$, since $K$ is locally integrable.

The convolved deterministic terms are $\sum_{i\le N}K_i(t)y_i^2$, which converge uniformly on compact subintervals of $(0,1]$ to $A_y(t)$ by its definition and bound above.

For a finite stochastic sum, stochastic Fubini gives $$K*\bigl(E_i*(QY_i\,dW_i)\bigr)(t)
       =\int_0^t K_i(t-v)Q(v)Y_i(v)\,dW_i(v).$$ It can first be used with $QY_i$ stopped at a finite bound. For such a bound a sufficient stochastic Fubini integral is at most $$C\int_0^t K(t-s)
       \left(\int_0^s E_i(s-v)^2\,dv\right)^{1/2}ds
 \le C\int_0^t K(t-s)\sqrt s\,ds<\infty.$$ Removing that bound by localization gives the displayed identity as local distributions.

To specify the limit without a formal exchange of infinite stochastic sums, for $C_0>0$ set $$q_{C_0}(v)=Q(v)\wedge(C_0v^{-1/4}),\qquad
 \zeta_{C_0}=\inf\{v>0:Q(v)>C_0v^{-1/4}\}.$$ By Lemma <a href="#entr:stochastic-kernels" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="entr:stochastic-kernels">30</a>, the partial sums of $\mathsf G_{q_{C_0}}^y+\mathsf N_{q_{C_0}}$ converge in probability in $C([0,1])$ on the whole probability space. Before $\zeta_{C_0}$, <a href="#entr:common-sde" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="entr:common-sde">[entr:common-sde]</a> gives $Y_i(v)=e^{-r_iv}y_i+Z_i^{q_{C_0}}(v)$, so these clipped partial sums agree there with the convolved finite stochastic sums.

Fix a deterministic $C_0>0$ and a rational $a\in(0,1]$. On the whole probability space, the clipped partial sums converge in probability in $C([0,a])$, and the convolved residual $K*(fR_N(X))$ converges in probability to zero in $L^1(0,a)$ as shown above. We may therefore choose a deterministic subsequence $N_j\uparrow\infty$ along which both convergences hold almost surely. Only then restrict to the event $\{a<\zeta_{C_0}\}$. On this event, passage in <a href="#entr:finite-constraint" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="entr:finite-constraint">[entr:finite-constraint]</a> proves <a href="#entr:volterra-equation" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="entr:volterra-equation">[entr:volterra-equation]</a> as a distribution on $(0,a)$. Take $C_0$ through the positive integers and $a$ through the rationals in $(0,1]$, and intersect the corresponding whole-space probability-one convergence events. The continuous versions then give equality for $0<t<\min\{\zeta_{C_0},1\}$, and by continuity at a positive hitting time $\zeta_{C_0}\le1$ and at $t=1$ when $\zeta_{C_0}>1$. The positive continuous $Q$ is finite at zero, and $\sup_{v\le1}v^{1/4}Q(v)<\infty$ almost surely. A sufficiently large integer $C_0$ therefore covers the whole interval. This proves the claimed identity and its precise interpretation. ◻

</details>

We next isolate the part of the equation that remembers the initial state. It becomes independent of that state when the weights <a href="#entr:seed-weights" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="entr:seed-weights">[entr:seed-weights]</a> escape.

<a id="stmt-entr-escaping-seeds"></a>
<div id="entr:escaping-seeds" class="lemma">

<a id="entr:A-limit"></a>
**Lemma 32** (Escaping seeds). *Suppose that, along a sequence of initial states possibly random, $\sum_i p_i=1$ and $p_i\to0$ in probability for every fixed $i$. Then $$\label{entr:A-limit}
 A_y\longrightarrow K
 \quad\text{in probability, uniformly on compact subintervals of \((0,1]\)}.$$ For each fixed $t>0$, the seed stochastic term $\mathsf G_q^y(t)$ tends to zero in $L^2$, uniformly over all adapted $q$ satisfying $|q(v)|\le C_0v^{-1/4}$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-entr-escaping-seeds"><summary>Proof of stmt-entr-escaping-seeds</summary>

*Proof.* By <a href="#entr:Ki-limit" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="entr:Ki-limit">[entr:Ki-limit]</a>, $2r_iK_i\to K$ uniformly on a fixed compact positive interval, and these functions are uniformly bounded there. In the convex combination $A_y=\sum_i p_i\,2r_iK_i$, the contribution of a fixed finite set tends to zero in probability and the contribution of its complement is uniformly close to $K$. This proves <a href="#entr:A-limit" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="entr:A-limit">[entr:A-limit]</a>.

For the stochastic assertion, its squared norm is at most $$C_{C_0}\int_0^t v^{-1/2}\,
       \mathbb E\!\left[\sum_i p_i r_i K_i(t-v)^2\right]\,dv .$$ For every $v<t$, <a href="#entr:Ki-bounds" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="entr:Ki-bounds">[entr:Ki-bounds]</a> implies $r_iK_i(t-v)^2\to0$, whereas <a href="#entr:Ki-sup" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="entr:Ki-sup">[entr:Ki-sup]</a> bounds it uniformly. Escape of $p_i$ makes the expression in brackets tend to zero in probability, and its uniform bound gives convergence of its expectation. Dominated convergence against $v^{-1/2}$ proves the assertion. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-33"></a>
#### Coupling entrances

We now prove the deterministic uniqueness and boundary assertions of Theorem <a href="#thm:entrance-selection" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:entrance-selection">27</a>. Work in unit time <a href="#entr:unit-time" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="entr:unit-time">[entr:unit-time]</a>. Let two proposed families be given, with starting sequences $u_{\ell,k}\downarrow0$, $\ell=1,2$. Start the diffusion of Lemma <a href="#entr:angular-realization" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="entr:angular-realization">28</a> from $\widetilde h^{\,\ell}_{u_{\ell,k}}\Pi$, and construct $(Q_\ell,f_\ell,Y_{\ell,i},y_{\ell,i})$ as above. Their seed weights escape in probability by <a href="#entr:escape" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="entr:escape">[entr:escape]</a> and <a href="#entr:seed-weights" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="entr:seed-weights">[entr:seed-weights]</a>. The constants below depend on $g$, and are uniform in $k$ and in the two families.

We may use the same Brownian motions for the two diffusions in elapsed time even though strong existence has not been asserted. Here is the coupling argument. Each joint law of the Brownian path $W$ and all its other continuous path variables is a probability on a standard Borel path space. Disintegrate it over $W$, and, given one Brownian path, sample the two other path variables independently from these conditional laws. Brownian motion remains Brownian in the joint filtration. To see this, if $\Phi_\ell$ is a bounded observable of the past of process $\ell$ through time $t$, independence of future Brownian increments in that process implies $$\mathbb E[\Phi_\ell\mid W\text{ on }[0,1]]
   =\mathbb E[\Phi_\ell\mid W\text{ on }[0,t]]
 \quad\text{almost surely}.$$ Test this equality first against products of functions of the Brownian past and future increments, and then use a monotone class argument. For a product $\Phi_1\Phi_2$, conditional independence in the coupling makes its conditional expectation the product of two functions of the Brownian past. A second monotone class argument proves independence of future increments from the joint past. Completion and right-continuous augmentation preserve this property. Finally, stochastic integrals are limits in probability of adapted simple sums. Their laws in each marginal are unchanged by the coupling, and they are the same integrals in this joint Brownian filtration. Thus all the preceding stochastic identities hold on the coupling.

<a id="pm-h-34"></a>
###### Stops with uniform failure bounds.

<a id="entr:seed-lower"></a>
Choose $C_0$ so large that $$C_0^2>1+\sup_{0<t\le1}\sup_y\sqrt t\,A_y(t),$$ where the supremum is over the normalized seeds in <a href="#entr:seed-weights" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="entr:seed-weights">[entr:seed-weights]</a>; it is finite by the bound on $A_y$ following Lemma <a href="#entr:kernels" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="entr:kernels">29</a>. For each solution use the clipped process $q_\ell^{\,0}(v)=Q_\ell(v)\wedge(C_0v^{-1/4})$. Let $k_0=\inf_{0<t\le1/2}\sqrt t\,K(t)>0$, and choose $c\in(0,k_0/4)$. Lemma <a href="#entr:escaping-seeds" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="entr:escaping-seeds">32</a> permits a deterministic sequence $\eta_k\downarrow0$, as slow as necessary, such that with probability tending to one both solutions satisfy $$\label{entr:seed-lower}
 \sqrt t\,A_{y_\ell}(t)\ge2c
             \qquad(\eta_k\le t\le1/2).$$ This follows by a diagonal choice from uniform convergence on each fixed compact interval.

Stop each solution when $\sqrt t\,f_\ell(t)$ first reaches the upper threshold $C_0^2$; it starts below that threshold since $f_\ell$ is finite at zero. Starting at $\eta_k$, also stop when $\sqrt t\,f_\ell(t)\le c$. Before the upper stop, Lemma <a href="#entr:volterra" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="entr:volterra">31</a> reads $$f_\ell=A_{y_\ell}
       +\mathsf G_{q_\ell^{\,0}}^{y_\ell}
       +\mathsf N_{q_\ell^{\,0}}.$$ It holds also at a positive first hit by continuity. On the event <a href="#entr:seed-lower" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="entr:seed-lower">[entr:seed-lower]</a>, either threshold hit by time $\delta\le1/2$ requires the supremum of the stochastic term on $[0,1]$ to be at least a fixed multiple of $\delta^{-1/2}$. Lemma <a href="#entr:stochastic-kernels" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="entr:stochastic-kernels">30</a> and Markov’s inequality therefore bound its probability by $C_j\delta^{j/2}$ for any fixed sufficiently large $j$, plus a term tending to zero with $k$.

Fix $0<\xi<1/4$. Add a stop for each solution at the infimum, over $i\ge1$, of the first times $$|Z_i^{q_\ell^{\,0}}(t)|\ge(1+r_i)^\xi.$$ This costs at most a positive power of $\delta$ by time $\delta$. Indeed if $N_i(t)=\sqrt2\int_0^t q_\ell^{\,0}(v)\,dW_i(v)$, integration by parts gives $$Z_i^{q_\ell^{\,0}}(t)
 =N_i(t)-r_i\int_0^t e^{-r_i(t-v)}N_i(v)\,dv,
 \qquad
 \sup_{t\le\delta}|Z_i^{q_\ell^{\,0}}(t)|
       \le2\sup_{t\le\delta}|N_i(t)|.$$ The last supremum has $L^j$ norm at most $C_j\delta^{1/4}$, uniformly in $i$. Choose $j>3/(2\xi)$, so $\sum_i(1+r_i)^{-j\xi}<\infty$ by <a href="#entr:rates" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="entr:rates">[entr:rates]</a>, and sum Markov’s inequality over $i$. The resulting bound is $C_j\delta^{j/4}$. A countable infimum of these stopping times is a stopping time in the right-continuous filtration.
