Gaussian tightness, proved in Proposition <a href="#prop:gaussian-subsequence" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:gaussian-subsequence">25</a> and Theorem <a href="#thm:entrance-selection" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:entrance-selection">27</a>, makes the right side of <a href="#repl:modulus-transfer" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="repl:modulus-transfer">[repl:modulus-transfer]</a> tend to zero as $\rho\downarrow0$ and makes the supremum tails vanish as their threshold tends to infinity. The Arzelà–Ascoli tightness criterion therefore gives tightness of the Rademacher restrictions to these rectangles.

Apply this argument on the exhaustion $[j^{-1},j]$ and $[j^{-1},j]^2$, $j\ge2$. The usual diagonal form of the same criterion gives tightness in the product of the two $C_{\mathrm{loc}}$ spaces. Every subsequential limit has the Gaussian finite-dimensional laws established above; evaluations on a countable dense set determine a law on continuous functions. The subsequential limit is therefore $\mathop{\mathrm{Law}}_g(A_g,B_g)$, proving Proposition <a href="#prop:universality" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:universality">46</a>.

Every query in the comparison used the original times $sT,tT$ and the original uniform initialization for $B_{n,J}$. The replacement changes only the coupling law. Thus the coefficient $c_*$ and the entrance $h_s^g$ obtained from the Gaussian construction pass unchanged to the Rademacher limit.

<a id="sec:completion"></a>
### Completion of the proof

<details id="proof-stmt-repl-comparison-2"><summary>Proof of stmt-repl-comparison</summary>

*Proof of Theorem <a href="#thm:main" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:main">1</a>.* In Gaussian disorder, Proposition <a href="#prop:edge-estimates" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:edge-estimates">3</a> supplies the cap estimates used in Theorem <a href="#thm:warming" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:warming">15</a>. Apply that theorem to the initial law $\nu_n$. Proposition <a href="#prop:gaussian-subsequence" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:gaussian-subsequence">25</a> then supplies, on a further represented subsequence of every sequence, a normalized positive-time density family for $S_t^g=e^{-tc_*H_g}$, together with locally uniform limits of both finite autocorrelations. Proposition <a href="#prop:uniform-seed-escape" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:uniform-seed-escape">26</a> gives the averaged uniform-start escape estimate. The sequence extraction and fixed-$g$ uniqueness in Theorem <a href="#thm:entrance-selection" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:entrance-selection">27</a> identify every represented family with the same measurable family $h^g$ for almost every $g$. The subsequence criterion gives the Gaussian joint convergence.

The density family is bounded at each positive time, hence belongs to $L^2(\Pi_g)$; it is nonnegative, has mass one, and satisfies the semigroup relation. Its weak product-topology boundary is $\delta_0$ by Theorem <a href="#thm:entrance-selection" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:entrance-selection">27</a>. Proposition <a href="#prop:gaussian-subsequence" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:gaussian-subsequence">25</a> proves the locally uniform convergence and continuity of the series defining $B_g$. Each finite partial sum is continuous in $(s,t)$, and its evaluations at rational pairs are measurable in $g$ by the density and semigroup constructions in Theorem <a href="#thm:entrance-selection" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:entrance-selection">27</a>. It is therefore Borel as a $C_{\mathrm{loc}}((0,\infty)^2)$-valued map, and so is its locally uniform limit.

Proposition <a href="#prop:gaussian-subsequence" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:gaussian-subsequence">25</a> gives $\|h_s^g-1\|_{L^2(\Pi_g)}\to0$, and hence the required $L^1$ convergence. It also gives locally uniform convergence $B_g(s,\cdot)\to A_g(\cdot)$ for almost every $g$ on which the selected family is defined. This implies the stated convergence in probability over $g$.

Proposition <a href="#prop:universality" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:universality">46</a> transfers the joint function law to Rademacher disorder. Its comparison uses the uniform initial law for each quench trace, so the limiting family is the one already selected in the Gaussian argument. The added Gaussian diagonal and the auxiliary eigenvector signs do not affect either finite autocorrelation. For both laws the finite dynamics use rate-one site clocks and are observed in the time unit $T_n=n^{2/3}$. The temporary substitution $u=c_*s$ was reversed in the entrance proof, so the limiting semigroup retains exactly the coefficient $c_*$ in <a href="#eq:edge-semigroup" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:edge-semigroup">[eq:edge-semigroup]</a>, completing all the assertions. ◻

</details>
